reviews.title: Hands Down the most Powerful Laptop I have used!
reviews.content:
The Asus ProArt P16 is a 16-inch 3K OLED touchscreen laptop. This laptop is powered by an AMD Ryzen 9 465 processor. This 10-core processor design handles multi-taking efficiently and effectively. This laptop contains dual graphics cards including an NVIDIA RTX 5060 card (with 8 GB of dedicated GDDR7 Graphics memory) and an AMD Radeon 880M graphics card (which uses up to 50% of the system RAM). This laptop’s main screen has a default resolution of 2880 by 1800 pixels. The laptop features 32 GB of RAM and 512 GB of hard drive space in the tested configuration.

For ports the laptop is outfitted on the left side with a power port for the AC power adapter, a full-sized HDMI 2.1 FRL (Full Rate Link) port, a USB 4.0 Gen 3 Type-C port with support for display/power delivery with a rated data speed of up to 40Gbps, and USB Gen 3.2 Type-A port with a rated speed of up to 10 Gbps, and a 3.5mm a headset Jack. The FRL HDMI port supports high-resolution external displays, including 8K output and high-refresh-rate 4K at 120Hz external monitors. The right side has a full-size SD Express 7.0 SD card slot, another USB Gen 3.2 Type-A port with a rated speed of up to 10 Gbps, and USB Gen 3.2 Type-C port with support for display/power delivery with a rated data speed of up to 40Gbps). The SD Card slot officially supports SDXC cards up to 2 TB and theoretically supports SDUC standards up to 128 TB as high-capacity cards become available. In a bit of an unusual placement the Power, Battery charge, and Drive activity lights are located on the rear of this laptop. This laptop weighs 4.08 lbs. and of course supports Wi-Fi 7 (BE standard) and Bluetooth 5.4. The battery is lithium-ion and is rated at ~ 90Wh. The laptop ships with a fast-charging 200W or 240W power adapter (reaching full charge in about 60 minutes) and supports USB-C charging between 45W and 100W.

This laptop is a CoPilot+ creator laptop that allows for on-device AI processing powered by the AMD XDNA NPU (up to 50 TOPS) and NVIDIA RTX AI acceleration supporting fast local creative tasks. This unit ships with ASUS StoryCube - an AI-assisted media hub that automatically organizes, categorizes, and tags local or cloud-synced photos and videos (with direct GoPro integration); ASUS MuseTree - an on-device AI generation tool that helps with brainstorming and creating images from text or sketches; and Microsoft Copilot is the pre-installed Windows AI companion for daily productivity and assistance

The laptop has impressive and immersive sound. I put it through my usual collection of these tracks that is handles with ease. This laptop’s sound is enhanced by Dolby Atmos capabilities to “surround you with lifelike sound depth and detail for music., movies, and more.”


Usage Impressions

Enough about the specifications, let’s talk usage impressions. First, the screen is gorgeous. Second, the two USB slots are both capable of supporting DisplayPort MST streaming hubs. In my testing the right USB-C and the left HDMI port were running via the NVIDIA RTX 5060 graphics card, the left UCB-C post and the main display of this laptop were running via the Radeon 880M graphics card. This dual graphics capability utilizes Microsoft Hybrid Graphics in conjunction with AMD SmartAccess Graphics to leverage the AMD Radeon Graphics card for basic low-power tasks like web browsing or text editing to save battery life and automatically switching to the NVIDIA RTX Graphics for heavy tasks like 3D Rendering, video export, or gaming.  Ias part of my testing, I was able to use two DisplayPort MST Hubs, and the HDMI Post to connect 7 external monitors and thus enabling a total of 8 screens! The 8 screens were running resolutions as follows: 3 at 1920x1080, 3 at 1920x1200, 2 at 3840x2160, and the main laptop at 2880 x 1800.  This is an impressive ability, even if it is a bit impractical / overkill for most users!

The last feature I am going to highlight is the massive 6” x4” Asus DialPad touchpad. This touchpad is configured with the ASUS Dial, a “precision-engineered rotary control providing intuitive fingertip mastery over app parameters and values. This dial enables one to work more efficiently with an array of applications via the rotary touch control. Examples of applications that can be control include but are not limited to Creative apps such as Adobe Photoshop, Adobe Premier Pro, and DaVinci Resole; Productivity apps such as Microsoft Word, Excel, and PowerPoint; Browsers like Chrome, Edge, and Firefox; entertainment apps such as Spotify, Netflix, and YouTube; and the Windows Operating system settings.  The configuration of the DialPad is managed thought the ASUS Control Panel Application.


Summary

The Asus ProArt P16 stands out as an exceptional desktop replacement and portable workstation for creators and developers. Powered by high-end specs and generous RAM, it easily handles demanding workflows. Highlights include unprecedented display connectivity—supporting up to 7 external monitors—and the integrated DialPad touchpad, which streamlines efficiency and creative control.

Key Strengths

 - Workstation Performance: Powerful CPU/GPU configurations and high RAM capacity effortlessly handle heavy computational and creative workloads.

 - Massive Display Output: Exceptional graphics support allowing up to 7 external monitors.

 - Streamlined Control: Built-in DialPad touchpad enhances workflow precision and overall productivity.

reviews.title: Exceptional Display for Creative Professionals
reviews.content:
I've been using the ASUS ProArt P16 as a secondary device for approximately two weeks, primarily for software development, AI development, and local LLM experimentation. My testing included running several Qwen 3.6 models as well as Gemma 4 models, largely to evaluate the capabilities of the Ryzen AI platform and the included NVIDIA GPU rather than as a dedicated AI workstation.

From a performance perspective, the laptop handled everyday development tasks very well. General responsiveness was excellent, builds felt snappy, and I did not encounter any noticeable slowdowns during normal use. Thermal performance was also impressive. Even when running local AI workloads, I did not observe meaningful fan noise, thermal throttling, or performance degradation over time.

For local AI use, the 32GB of RAM is adequate but not ideal if that is your primary workload. The system was capable of running the models I tested, but inference speeds were not particularly remarkable. More importantly, 32GB leaves limited headroom as newer and larger models continue to grow. Similarly, the included 512GB SSD may become restrictive for AI enthusiasts, as individual models can consume 20-30GB or more of storage. It works, but prospective buyers should understand this limitation.

The standout feature of this laptop is unquestionably the display. The 16-inch 3K OLED touchscreen is one of the most impressive laptop displays I have personally used. The colors are exceptionally vivid, and the quality is immediately apparent from the moment the system boots. Whether viewing media, working with design assets, or simply spending long hours coding, the screen is excellent. ASUS clearly prioritized display quality, and it shows.

The keyboard and trackpad are perfectly serviceable but do not stand out from competing premium laptops. The creator-focused dial integrated into the trackpad is an interesting idea and will likely appeal to artists and designers, although I did not personally incorporate it into my workflow.

Portability was another pleasant surprise. Given the 16-inch display, I expected something closer to a desktop replacement. Instead, the ProArt P16 feels noticeably lighter and more portable than expected. Carrying it around was never an issue, and it strikes a nice balance between screen size and mobility.

Battery life, connectivity, and port selection were all solid without calling attention to themselves. Nothing felt lacking, but nothing dramatically exceeded expectations either.

Overall, this is a very capable laptop with an absolutely exceptional display. However, I'm not convinced that the display alone justifies the premium price for every buyer. For software developers, general productivity users, or those with lighter creative needs, there are more affordable machines that will accomplish similar tasks. On the other hand, serious digital artists, designers, and creative professionals who can truly take advantage of the OLED touchscreen and creator-focused features should give the ProArt P16 strong consideration. For that audience, it is one of the most compelling options I've seen.

reviews.title: Swiss army knife of laptops
reviews.content:
I have never had a laptop that was marketed as a creative device. This unit functions well in use for day-to-day processing and gaming (surprisingly). I was concerned about its 16-inch size as I tend more towards 14 inches or less (nice for traveling) but it’s somewhat svelte 4-pound aluminum case converted me. 

Under that dark no smudge (that really works) aluminum case we find

AMD Ryzen AI 9 465 (2026) processor featuring 10 cores (4 Zen 5 and 6 Zen 5c cores), 20 threads with up to 5.0 GHz(?). It’s important to note the year of processor as costs have seen some manufacturers using older processors.
Dedicated XDNA 2 Neural Engine delivering 50 TOPS
Radeon 880M dedicated iGPU. Its allocated memory can be changed using the MyAsus app.
NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 dGPU with 8GB GDDR7 memory.
32GB of LPDDR5X 8000(!) MHz memory. Not upgradable.
512GB Micron PCIe NVMe M.2 4.0 SSD. 
OLED 16-inch 3K touchscreen. 2880 x 1800, 60 or 120HZ with 500NITS and 100% Color Gamut(NTSC).
Wi-fi 7
8ft 200-watt inline smallish power cord/block using Asus small oblong connector. You can also charge using USB-C ports.

1x 3.5mm Combo Audio Jack, 
1x HDMI 2.1 FRL, 
2x USB-A 3.2 (data speed up to 10Gbps).
1x USB-C 3.2 (data speed up to 10Gbps)
1x USB-C 4 (data speed up to 40Gbps) with DisplayPort and power delivery
1x SD card reader – secure digital

That is a lot to like, but how does this all work in the real world? 

As this is not a gaming laptop there is no color palate to set on keyboard. But keyboard is backlit and I liked the soft touch keys with a nice tactile feel. On top left of touchpad there is also a DialPad which using ProArt Creator Hub allows you to customize functions. I must be getting old as I tried to use it but honestly don’t get why its there. 

The OLED screen is great. Colors really pop but screen is pretty reflective (as is the case with most touchscreens) especially if dark background on screen. You can select 60 or 120Hz response. Lower Asus power settings will automatically change 60 from 120.

You can pretty much tweak/check every processing component aspect using the MyAsus app.

For productivity there is StoryCube which can use AI to help with your pictures/videos/audio.  There is also MuseTree which also uses AI for creating visual concepts that you can manipulate. Nice thing is it runs offline. I must admit I am still not sure how these work but they were fun to “play” with initially. Glidex can connect the laptop to other devices – I connected my phone and it worked okay but need to use it more. There is also ScreenXpert and CapCut which I didn’t try.

Power button is on the top right of keyboard, by itself, making it really hard to accidentally turn it off.

4-cell Lithium-ion battery was impressive. Using best power efficiency setting and iGPU with VLC app looping a stored movie (1920x1080P 24FPS 7060kbps) I clocked 13 hours with 8% battery life left. This was with Wi-fi and Bluetooth on using wireless headphones. Using balanced power mode and checking email/surfing I clocked 5 hours with 13% battery left (also had Wi-fi and Bluetooth on). Very impressive numbers.

Wifi 7 (802.11be) worked great with my wifi 7 system.

I ran productivity tests as well as gaming and this machine can handle both pretty well with nice frame rates (see attachments).

The SD slot is nice for easily added storage or accessing your data. I would have preferred a Micro-sd as that slides completely into the case. 

No Thunderbolt port as it seems Thunderbolt is licensed by Intel. 

No ethernet connection.

I have used NVIDIA GPU for years and knew there were 2 drivers - Gaming and Studio but didn’t know why. In researching the difference - gaming drivers are updated frequently to keep up with new/updated games. Studio drivers are updated less frequently and allow for a more stable environment for creative applications. Who knew?

1-year warranty.

Coming in with just a 512GB SSD was initially irritating, especially given this units price point. But the market is crazy right now – in October 2025 I purchased a 2TB drive from BB – that exact same drive10 months later is 3 times as expensive. This is where we are at right now and would rather have the 32GB of memory and the dGPU. The SSD is the easiest component to upgrade (if/when prices come down). I actually had a 1TB SSD I was using as a USB stick (the one the 2TB replaced) and I easily switched it out replacing the 512GB.

There are so many things to like about this laptop. Surprising gaming performance and battery life. If you are looking for the portable army knife of laptops WITH a touchscreen - this is one I would recommend.

reviews.title: Fast, Beautiful, and Built for Creative Work (Desp
reviews.content:
As someone who works extensively with Adobe Creative Suite and has used a Surface Laptop Studio 2 for a few years, you can imagine I was eager to upgrade to something faster and more agile. The ASUS ProArt P16 has been an amazing replacement workhorse so far, thanks to its beautiful 120Hz OLED display, the unique DialPad perfect for creative professionals, and excellent battery life.
 
PROS
- Beautiful OLED display with excellent color accuracy out of the box (plus it's a touchscreen!)
- Excellent performance thanks to the AMD Ryzen AI 9 465 processor, 32 GB RAM, and (very important) the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 GPU
- Great port selection with two USB-C ports (one on each side, which is convenient YKIYK), USB-A, HDMI, and an SD card reader
- Comfortable chiclet-style keyboard
 
CONS
- Large power brick with a proprietary charging port (you can still charge via USB-C, thankfully)
- Diving board-style trackpad feels old-school. You'd think it'd be haptic at this price point!
- So many ventilation openings on the bottom (not great for appearance and a note for cooling)
 
OVERVIEW
Right off the bat, this is a pretty attractive laptop with minimal branding and a sleek matte black finish. It is a fingerprint magnet, though, so you'll be constantly cleaning it if fingerprints bother you. Be careful about where you position this bad boy because of all the ventilation slots at the bottom. Putting it directly on something like a bed can cause it to overheat really fast. Opening and closing the lid with one hand is a cinch thanks to the angled lid and smooth hinge. I didn’t experience much wobble with the display, so I consider it fairly sturdy. 
 
The keyboard is wide and extremely comfortable to type on. The trackpad is very large and has a glass surface. I only wish it were haptic with no moving parts, like other higher-priced laptops. The ASUS DialPad is a great feature that I'm still getting used to, but so far it's been nice to have when the laptop is open or out and about.
 
When it comes to performance, this is where I feel like I'm in the future coming from my older laptop. It is incredibly snappy, handling multitasking without any hesitation. I honestly rarely hear the fans power up to a point where it's distracting, but then again, I'm generally with my earbuds in. That said, I wouldn't consider this a loud computer compared to my older Surface Laptop Studio 2, where I frequently heard the fans kick up. 
 
At 512 GB, storage might be a little tight for some, but I imagine most creatives are working from a USB-C drive (or I am at least), so I don't think it would be too much of an issue.
 
Port selection is another highlight offering plenty of options for most people, including USB-A (which is seemingly rare these days) and a SD card slot (no dongles needed!). 
 
I will knock ASUS, though, for the dumb decision to include a power brick with a proprietary charging port. Yes, you can absolutely charge the laptop via one of the two USB-C ports. I keep the power brick at my desk, but I use my Anker 140W USB-C charger when I'm on the go because it's more useful than the included power brick. Speaking of power, while your mileage will vary based on what you're doing, I seem to average between 6 and 8 hours, depending on the intensity of the photo editing and graphic design work I do. If you do more Office work and web browsing, I'm sure you might get a little more.
 
Overall, the ProArt P16 has been a fantastic creator laptop with one of the best laptop displays I've used, excellent performance, and a premium feel. If you can overlook some of the cons or gripes I mentioned, I think you will be very pleased with your decision to pick this bad boy up.

reviews.title: 120Hz panel but slower write speed 512GB SSD
reviews.content:
Design
From looks and weight, there is virtually no change between the 2026 model and its last 2 models. Whatever changes there are, I haven't noticed them.
Made from an aluminum body, it’s lightweight, but feels solid and durable, with no creaking or flexing under normal use. Its black finish is attractive and fingerprint resistant. It doesn’t feel metallic and feels comfortable on the skin, soft and silky smooth. The status lights are curiously found on the back of the laptop and hidden by the hinge when the display is folded open. It only seems to be useful while the laptop isn’t in use. The keyboard is backlit with 3 levels of brightness and the option to turn the backlight off. However, I found the minimum setting for the backlight to be too bright. The backlight also doesn’t illuminate the Shift function labels on the keys. The keyboard itself has considerably more travel than other ultra slim laptops, while still being silent. There is no numpad, but this allows for front-firing speakers on the sides of the keyboard as well as the touchpad in a centered position, to prevent accidental input while typing while looking straight on to the screen. The P16 comes with an infrared camera compatible with Windows Hello for facial recognition login, which works in the dark, and more convenient than fingerprint login. 

Display
The display is a glossy touch screen OLED with slim bezels and measures 15.8” diagonally. It’s pretty reflective, so it’s not ideal for use opposite a window or light source. Its native resolution is 2880x1800 this time. Branded as a 3K display, it's a downgrade from the usual 3840x2400, but keeps its 16:10 aspect ratio. It’ll produce black bars for 16:9 presentations, but the extra vertical space makes it better for content creation, giving you a larger workspace. Because it’s a 3k display against a 16” display, you'll be able to spot individual pixels at 150% scale but only if you look really close at the screen. This model introduces a 120Hz touch display to the ProArt P16 line which is great for gaming and any high frame rate video editing. The hinge only folds back as far as 130°. There’s also some wobble when the display is touched. It also does not come with a stylus although it supports the ASUS stylus. When I tried using my Samsung phone’s S-pen, it wouldn’t work. I found the touch display best for making quick selections in editing programs with buttons like Photoshop, and keep the touchpad in my editing workspace. Since the hinge doesn’t fold flat to 180° or 360°, the P16 doesn’t work well for drawing with touch input. I didn’t notice any text fringing. The display is Dolby Vision certified, and is able to play Dolby Vision content. It's probably because of the new 120Hz 3K panel, but unlike the previous 2 models, the colors don't look as oversaturated out of the box. Still creators looking for accurate colors will want to switch to a different profile such as sRGB, which is great for web content, or Display P3, which is great for graphics and video editing.

Inputs
Charging is done from the left side of the laptop, and the only way to take advantage of the P16 at full power is using the stock 200W power adapter. The USB 4 port only charges at up to 100W, which will cap the CPU and GPU. The cap isn’t as bad as it sounds because it’s still a powerful laptop even with the cap. You just won’t be able to take full advantage of the hardware’s capability. Due to this being a Ryzen laptop, one of its USB-C ports is only USB 4 and not a Thunderbolt port. ASUS also skimps out compared to the competition by making its other USB-C port 3.2. This USB 3.2 Type-C port on the right side has power delivery, but isn’t capable of charging the laptop. 

Connectivity
It comes with WiFi 7 but unfortunately maxes out at 2882MB/s up&down. I've seen others do 5000MB/s. It also has Bluetooth 5.4.

Performance
When set to Performance mode, which can only be run while plugged in using the stock 200W charger, the P16 is impressively powerful, but the fans blare non-stop, making it a pretty noisy laptop. It’s not a high-pitched sound or anything offensive, but it’s a noticeably aggressive sound of fans spinning. The laptop doesn’t get too hot as long as the vents on the bottom of the laptop aren’t blocked. It’s best used on a flat desk and not recommended on a bed while in Performance mode. 

While in Performance mode, I was able to play Shadow of the Tomb Raider in max Custom settings, which is more demanding than its preset Ultra settings in native 2880x1800 resolution and get a stable 90fps. In 1080p with those same maxed out settings, I could get 116fps (a drop from last year's RTX 5070 that gave me 144fps). Thanks to the 120Hz panel, you can game with frame rates higher than 60fps for games that allow it. For content creation, 120 Hz isn't needed unless you're working with videos with high frame rate. Sadly, the display has no variable refresh rate (VRR). It can only output at 60Hz or 120Hz. In the ASUS settings, it has "adaptive refresh rate" which only switches between 60Hz (battery) and 120Hz (plugged), depending on whether a power source is connected or not. That is NOT VRR.

When running on battery, the P16 caps its CPU, and the discrete GPU (if it's being used). The P16 will use the integrated Radeon 880M, which is a downgrade from last year's 890M. But keep in mind, last year's model had a 4K panel to drive. This model is only a 3K panel. I never experienced any thermal throttling.

Other than Performance mode, the laptop runs cool and very silent, especially in Whisper mode, where the fan never seems to go off. Through the MyASUS app, your hardware configuration is customizable. You can run on the integrated graphics card exclusively for longer battery life. It’s also nice that the integrated graphics is a Radeon variant (880M), while the discrete GPU is a GeForce RTX 5060, particularly for software that has benefits for one type over the other. 

Unfortunately, the SSD is a downgrade from last year's model.
While still speedy with a 5210 MB/s sequential read, 3293 MB/s sequential write, it's down from 5279/4831, respectively. The huge drop in write speed is the most glaring. Its random read of 41 MB/s and random write of 93 MB/s from 56/146, respectively. Perhaps the most unforgivable is that the storage size is 512GB. If you edit high resolution videos like I do, and especially, if you're a gamer, 512GB fills up quick. Final Fantasy VII Rebirth takes up 159GB. Marvel Tokon takes up 25.5GB. The OS itself takes up 35GB. Replacing the SSD yourself costs a fortune these days, which is probably the reason for the downgrade with this model.
There is a spare m.2 slot for additional SSD storage.

While it uses current gen CPU HX 465, it downgrades the family of the model (last year was a HX 370). With that comes a minor drop in performance.
Cinebench 2024
plugged in
CPU multi core: 969 (down from 1185)
CPU single core: 112 (down from 116)
  MP Ratio: 8.68x (down from 10.20x)

Battery 
Using the 200W stock power adapter, it takes 1 hour and 45 minutes to charge from 0% to 100%, though it hits around the 90% mark after around 1 hour. Using a 100W USB-C charger, took about 4 hours to charge from 0% to 100% but hit around 90% after around 1 hour and 30 minutes. The battery life itself varies greatly depending on the mode you use and what you’re doing but otherwise excellent when you need it to be without the laptop feeling sluggish. When streaming video non-stop at 100% brightness and 50% volume I got about 9 hours of battery life. When gaming in 3K using the discrete GPU in 120Hz display mode with HDR on and no caps (Windows mode; Best Performance power plan) it lasted only 54 minutes.

Sound
The sound was amazing. It utilizes Dolby Atmos, which gives the audio depth without sacrificing detail. The speakers also get very loud without any distortion. The microphone on the other hand isn’t very impressive. My recorded voice sounds too processed and unnatural. Turning off the noise cancellation makes the sound of my voice more natural but the audio quality still sounds bad. It sounds like AM radio. It does do a good job with noise cancellation though, eliminating sounds like an air conditioner, fan, and even TV that's playing something in the background.

Touchpad 
The touchpad is very responsive but unfortunately lacks haptic feedback. Taps can be done anywhere on the touchpad, but physical button clicks can only be done on the bottom portion. The touchpad is very responsive and feels smooth to touch. It has a unique DialPad touch feature built in to the top-left portion of the touchpad that needs to activated via a simple drag from the top-right corner of the touchpad gesture. I have never accidentally triggered this gesture personally, although perhaps your mileage may vary. When the DialPad is turned on, it gives you a touch dial that comes with preset functions for specific apps like Photoshop and Word, while also allowing you to customize the dial with functions and apps that you assign on your own. This gives your shortcut access to commonly used functions via the DialPad.

The main attraction for this year's ProArt P16 vs previous years is the 120Hz panel. However, it seems that it falls victim to the state of high priced RAM and SSDs. I'm thankful that it's still giving us 32GB RAM, which is nonupgradeable. But the storage size is where the ProArt P16 pays a heavy price with only 512GB and a slower write speed. It's no longer an easy recommendation to get like it used to be but a lot of what people love about this ProArt P16 still remains. I recommend it but beware of the cons.

Pros:
-Excellent color reproduction
-16:10 ratio screen
-Excellent loud sound without distortion
-bright backlit keys with good contrast
-no thermal throttling
-runs cool
-light for its size and power (4 lbs)
-Windows Hello face login

Cons:
-512GB SSD with slower write speeds than previous years
-No variable refresh rate

reviews.title: Gets the job done well
reviews.content:
I’ve really been enjoying the ASUS ProArt P16 so far. This is one of those laptops that feels premium as soon as you start using it, but what I like most is that it actually has the performance to back up the look. The 16” 3K OLED touchscreen is probably my favorite feature. The display is absolutely beautiful. Everything looks sharp, colors are vibrant, and the contrast is really impressive. Whether I’m working, browsing, watching Netflix, or just doing everyday things, the screen makes everything look better. The touchscreen is also a nice bonus and makes navigating around the laptop really convenient.

Performance has been excellent. With the AMD Ryzen AI 9 processor and 32GB of RAM, this thing handles multitasking with no problem. I can have several browser tabs and programs open at the same time without it slowing down or feeling like it’s struggling. Everything feels quick and responsive, which is exactly what I want from a laptop at this price point. The 512GB SSD also keeps things moving quickly while giving me a good amount of storage for my everyday needs.

I really like the design too. The Nano Black finish looks sleek and professional without being boring. For a 16” laptop with this much power, it also doesn’t feel as bulky as I expected. It still feels like something I could easily take with me when I need to work somewhere other than home.

The Copilot+ PC features are a nice addition as well. I’m still exploring everything the AI features can do, but I like having those newer capabilities built into the laptop rather than feeling like I’m using an older computer that’s already behind the times.

Overall, I think ASUS did a really good job with the ProArt P16. The display is gorgeous, the performance is fast, the touchscreen is useful, and the overall design feels very premium. It’s not just a laptop that looks good sitting on a desk—it actually performs really well too. I think this would be a great choice for someone who wants something powerful enough for creative work and multitasking but still wants a laptop that’s enjoyable to use for everyday things like streaming, browsing, and general productivity. So far, I’ve been very impressed with it.

reviews.title: A great laptop made for creators.
reviews.content:
A great laptop made for creators, and AI enthusiasts who need workstation-class performance in a portable package. 

Unpacking and setup.
The laptop came nicely packed in double boxes; the original box contains charger and another smaller box that packs only laptop. The laptop then nicely wraps in paper/fabric cushioned packaging giving it a premium feel. 

Build quality:
It is solid build and has a clean, premium design that fits perfectly in an office or studio. An outstanding 3K OLED Display with touch capability that is very responsive, but that making the screen more reflective which I did not like. Although the specification says anti reflective coating, but I find it still more reflecting than it should be.
The touch pad has an inbuilt wheel/creator wheel/dial pad that can be used with Photoshop and lightroom and customizable with other applications. Tough pas is soft and easy to click and touch responsive. The keyboard is very easy to type with sufficient key travel and feels natural. 

Connectors/ports:
It uses a specific USB C like proprietary charging port but also has a USB 4 port with 40GBPS that can be used for high-speed data transfer and charging, to docking station.  A Full-size SD card reader that is for easy photo transfer, an HDMI port and 2 USB A and 2 USB C port and an audio combo jack. It lacks the fingerprint button which I feel it could have been included.

Performance: photo/video editing in lightroom, photoshop.
It packs AMD Ryzen AI 9 CPU and 32GB RAM with NVIDIA RTX 5060 Laptop GPU that find sufficient for demanding workloads with ease. A 500 GB internal storage will quickly fill up it should have at least 1TB, but I think may be due the shortage of the storage devices ausus decided to stick to a satisfactory 500gb. It also supports modern AI features and hardware acceleration for AI applications. 
 It performs exceptionally well in with Photoshop And lightroom with AI filters in my experience. The battery lasted for about 4 hours with full brightness and an external 4K monitors connected. The color correction needed to be performed to get the accurate color. The out of the box color are good for everyday use. For longer demanding run it becomes a bit hot but that is acceptable and if kept on laptop stand with sufficient space for easy venting of heat or a laptop cooler would be good. 

Overall, The ASUS ProArt P16 strikes an excellent balance between portability, creative performance, AI capability, and premium design. It’s gorgeous OLED display, strong CPU/GPU combination, and creator-focused features make it a great laptop in its class. It comfortably handles demanding workloads while remaining elegant enough for professional environments. Although it has a windows halo, but I miss a fingerprint scanner, and the screen is reflective. Other than these two the laptop is a solid build.

reviews.title: Wow on the display and sound!!
reviews.content:
The display is what blew me away first. The image is sharp, the color is vivid and vibrant, everything just pops out, and it uses a very bright OLED panel. 

The laptop speakers are also very impressive. They are very loud, have full-body sound and good bass, and the sound quality is very good, almost reaching the audiophile level. The sax music I played sounds so warm. 

With a high-end CPU, AMD Ryzen AI 9 465, and NVIDIA RTX 5060 dedicated graphics card, I believe this is the slimmest laptop out there with this level of performance, and it is not heavy at all, weighing only 4 lbs. The power brick weighs 1.15 lbs. 

Even though it is slim and compact, the build quality is top-notch. The hinge is sturdy, and there is no flex in the body or even the display. 

The full-size keyboard has good travel and spacing and is very comfortable to type on. However, there is no Home button, no Page Up or Page Down button, and only one button where the Delete and Insert keys share. 

The touchpad is well built and has a built-in dial pad. It is convenient in a pinch, but I prefer to use an actual bigger physical dial pad. 

The laptop has many ports, but the power-in port is non-standard. Even though it does charge using the USB-C port, a pop-up dialog will appear letting you know it is charging slowly and recommends using the included power brick. 

The included SSD is from Micron and is very fast, able to get more than 700 MB/s when installing a game. 

The Wi-Fi speed is also very fast for this laptop. 

Besides all the useful ports, this laptop has a full-size SD card slot with fast transfer speed. 

Temperature management is very good. While unplugged, the back measured 108°F and the top above the keyboard measured 107°F. When plugged in doing light-duty work, the back rose to 112°F. When playing games, the back rose to 124°F. 

While not playing games, it is not noisy at all, even when plugged in. 

Battery life is very good as well; watching video while unplugged, the battery went from 100% to 80% in one hour. 

This laptop is ideal for gaming as well, not just for creators. 

ASUS includes these AI apps: StoryCube to organize media with AI and MuseTree to create images using AI. You can use the included ProArt Creator Hub app to access system metrics and system configuration. 

The built-in camera is a bit soft but does support Windows Hello, which is a plus. 

There are only two things I don't like: the status lights are at the back bottom of the display panel, so it is not possible to see them while the display panel is opened, and the arrow keys are half-height size.

reviews.title: Sleek and Surprisingly Versatile.
reviews.content:
The ASUS - ProArt P16 16" 3K OLED Touchscreen Laptop - AMD Ryzen AI 9 465 (2026) - 32GB RAM - 512GB SSD - Copilot+ PC - Nano Black meets all my needs and then some.  Unpackaging was a great experience.  The meticulous packaging with all black design was impressive.  One could say the packaging was on the verge of mimicking a Russian nesting doll.  It did build the anticipation of getting to the prize of finally holding the sleek P16 in my hands.  The physical design is sleek and beautifully simple.  The military grade aluminum design is pretty cool.  Even though, I do not plan on taking my laptop off road with me, it is good to know it can take a hit if the situation ever arose.  The backlit keyboard is bright and lights up to three times brightness if needed. There is also a hotkey for copilot which is perfect since I have been using AI more and more as the technology has improved. The ASUS DialPad is a nice addition to the touchpad.  The touchpad is huge and works great when you do not have a mouse on the go.  The touchpad combined with the DialPad pretty much replaces a mouse and helps out tremendously when I take my laptop to work.  I wanted to start learning how to create content and edit video and this DialPad will work with creative applications so it is good to know that I do not have to purchase separate devices for editing. 

The 16” touchscreen OLED 4K picture is unrivaled.  With 120Hz refresh rate and up to 1,600 nits I can even watch a movie or play a high graphic demand game if I wanted.  What is more, the Harman Kardon 6 speaker audio system makes movies and games immersive. The surround sound replaces the need to go to the movies.  I also plan to use my laptop for teaching remote classes.  The web camera and studio grade microphone provide full HD picture and AI assisted video and noise cancellation. This should be a welcome change for my students for the upcoming Fall semester.  The ProArt Creator Hub is nifty and I really like the work smart feature.  I can combine my favorite applications into a work group which makes work more efficient.  If you are unorganized, like me, and have ever spent time hitting the windows icon and scrolling through your apps for over a minute to find a needed app during work, the WorkSmart feature is for you.  If needed, the ProArt Creator Hub also allows you to give applications priority for power use.  The available ports on this sleek laptop are perfect.  This laptop features 2 HDMI type A, 2 HDMI type C, Headset Audio, and an SD Card port.  There is no need to buy a docking station or port extender.  This PC is perfect for uploading drone or GoPro footage on the go.  Battery life can vary depending on the applications you are running.  For standard use, I have gone around 8+ hours without needing to plug in.  Overall, I am very impressed with the design, touchscreen & high-quality picture-in-one, sound output and quality, battery life, and port availability.

reviews.title: Great Laptop for Creators
reviews.content:
This is the best laptop that I have used to date and has very few weaknesses for my workload.

KEY SPECIFICATIONS

PROCESSOR: The CPU is a 10 core / 20 thread AMD Ryzen AI 9 465 with integrated Radeon 880M graphics. Performance is about 17% better than an older Intel Core i7-12700H mobile processor (14 core / 20 thread) per the Passmark CPU benchmarks.

GRAPHICS: Besides the integrated graphics, there is also a dedicated RTX 5060 with 8gb of memory.  Performance is comparable to an RTX 5050 desktop GPU per benchmarks I’ve seen.
MEMORY: 32 GB of LPDDR5X memory.  This memory is very fast.  Faster than the DDR5 I have in my desktop PC.  It is also soldered to the motherboard and not upgradable.  That’s OK.  It is enough for the tasks I use. 

STORAGE DRIVE(S):  My laptop came with a 512 GB (QLC), m.2, PCIe 4x4 drive by Micron.  It’s not a great drive.  This is probably the most disappointing part of this laptop.  QLC memory is not as durable as TLC typically and is used mostly in budget drives.  My tests gave me Seq. Read Speeds of 5069 MB/s and Write Speeds of 3316 MB/s.  While OK, it’s a bit disappointing for a high-end Media Creator’s computer.  This will be replaced soon.  There is an additional m.2 slot so you can expand storage if you are willing to open the case.  

SUBJECTIVE RATINGS

CHASSIS / LOOKS: 10/10
Looks Great.  ProArt products tend to have a clean, simple look.  This laptop is no exception.  The cover is all black with a small, embossed ASUS ProArt logo in the corner.  It is extremely thin and light for a laptop with this much power.  I had a gaming laptop with similar specs and it was noticeably bulkier.  I wouldn’t consider it ultralight at about 4 lbs, but I haven’t seen an ultralight laptop with RTX 5060 graphics.  Despite being so thin, there is very little flex to the body.  The lid opens with a single finger with just enough effort.  The bezels around the monitor are very thin.  It is very well done.

MONITOR: 10/10
It is probably the best monitor I’ve seen on a laptop.  Video filmed in and viewed in 4k is crystal clear and just flat out stunning.  Contrast is as good as it can get.  Colors really pop.  Everything you expect from an OLED monitor.  Details can be seen that are missed on the 1200p monitors that are typical in laptops with this size monitor.  Oh yea… It’s also a touch screen that works great if it’s something you would use.

KEYBOARD: 7/10
The keyboard is also very good. The lettering is very clear.  The backlight illuminates the letters, so they are easy to see.  There are 3 brightness levels and the backlight could also be turned off.  The media buttons are dominant over the F keys out of the box.   However, the F-Keys can be made dominant by pressing the Fn-Esc keys.  I don’t like the CoPilot button that removes the CTRL key on the right side of the keyboard.  I am left-handed and use the left CTRL-INS key combination to copy.  I can’t use that combination because this key was removed.  I also don’t like the shared DEL-INS key.  I also wish there was a numeric keypad to the right but the tradeoff is quality sound from the front facing speakers.

TRACKPAD: 9/10
The Trackpad is very large and responsive.  Both in terms of pointer movement and tapping.  There is also a unique circle in the upper left hand corner that acts as a dial.  In different programs it has different uses. 

WEBCAM:  8/10
Picture is as good as any of the better webcams I’ve used.  No complaints.

SPEAKERS: 9/10
No need for external speakers.  Best sounding laptop I’ve ever used.  While not as good as a decent dedicated 2.1 speaker set, it is better than I thought I would ever hear on a laptop.  Past experiences have been so terrible, I always carried a small Bluetooth speaker with my laptop when I traveled.  I don’t need that anymore. 

PERFORMANCE: 8.5/10
It runs everything I need it to without issue.  During general use, the PC will use the low power GPU.  If more power is needed, the PC will switch over to the dedicated RTX 5060 with 8gb of memory.  While not as powerful as its desktop counterpart, it is more than capable for most creative tasks.  (If more power is needed, the P16 is available with faster GPU’s.)  When using the RTX GPU, the fans can get noticeable.  During less graphics intensive work, the laptop is quiet.  Storage is limited with the 512 gb drive and it could be faster.  Additional storage is needed if editing multiple, longer videos. I’ve already filled half the drive with the programs I’ve installed.

CONNECTIVITY:  
There are two (2) USB 3.2 Type A ports, one (1) USB 3.2 Type C port and one (1) USB 4.0 Type C port.  There is also an HDMI port, an SD card reader and a combo headphone / mic jack.  The USB 4.0 port works great with both my portable monitors.  I’ve had issues with another laptop but none with this one.
 
INCLUDED SOFTWARE:
It comes with several Asus Programs. Some for creatives, some utilities.   There is MyAsus,  the laptop control software that lets you see performance, temperatures, laptop specs, critical driver updates and much more.  There are free trials for McAfee Internet Security, MS Office, Xbox and some Adobe Products.  

CONCLUSION:
This is one of Asus’s Flagship laptops.  It is the entry level ProArt, but it is still very powerful and extremely well built.  It works great for what it is designed for, Media Creation.  It just needs some additional storage.  If you are in the market for something like this, the ProArt line is a great place to look.

reviews.title: Solid PC, no pen included? How?!
reviews.content:
I waited a long time for this device to release, extremely excited for a Surface Pro alternative with more power, all of the features I was looking for in a creative-centered device in the most flexible form factor available. The PC overall is exactly what I was hoping for, but with one massive miss. 

All marketing for this PC included the stylus, the ASUS Pen 3.0, and stressed the quality, functionality, and experience. I was absolutely blown away to open the box after ordering on release day to find no stylus included. Something had to be wrong, as every review I'd seen had the stylus included in the box, and it's use was so aggressively advertised everywhere I'd seen reference to the PC. It's a tablet Windows PC, after all, designed for creatives. The rear cover has the pen holder integrated. There's no way that they'd sell it in other markets including the stylus, but leave it out in the US, right?

I reached out to ASUS and they confirmed that the model number includes the stylus. Connected with Best Buy per ASUS's recommendation and was told that it's not part of the package. Reach back out to ASUS, open tickets, multiple phone calls, chat sessions, emails, and finally received a response that they do NOT include the Pen 3.0 in the US release. When I expressed my frustration and asked what the solution would be, I was told that it's not available to purchase on it's own. I couldn't possibly be more blown away at how horrible of a decision this is on the part of ASUS. To then be told "we're sorry, that's frustrating, have a good day" by ASUS support has completely changed my view of the company. 

I've owned ASUS products for many, many years. This is very likely to be my last, if I end up keeping it. I wouldn't have questioned the purchase for a moment if it was $50 more and included the stylus, I can't wrap my head around the decisions made that lead to the exclusion of it in this package. Beyond that, to have absolutely zero solution in place for a customer to purchase the Pen 3.0 just shows that the priority isn't on the customer experience and overall satisfaction, and when ASUS misses the mark, they don't really care. 

If you value the ability to use a stylus that integrates well into the package (I've purchase a third party device that rattles around in the compartment as the magnetic point isn't in the right location) you'll want to look elsewhere. Of course, there are older versions of ASUS pens available, but they're expensive and fall short of the intended experience per ASUS's marketing. Spend a bit more for a very similar Surface Pro option where you have to buy your own keyboard and pen? Buy a more "standard laptop" configuration? I'm not sure of the answer as this was so very close to my perfectly ideal solution, but as of this moment I'm unable to use the device in the way that I was lead to believe I'd be able to.

reviews.title: Didn’t last a year
reviews.content:
I had high hopes for this laptop. This was my first “adult” laptop purchase (always been provided with one through school or work) and I did an immense amount of research on all types of laptops before purchasing. I wanted something I could use for work and had the storage for all the things I need plus some more, and I wanted something I could use a smart pen with to write, scroll, read and create artwork. This is why I loved the capabilities of the Asus Zenbook Duo 13” laptop. Unfortunately, it didn’t live up to the hype.
Issues I had with this laptop (note* it was kept clean, no spills, no drops, no damages, etc.) 
1. The biggest issue - the second screen just STOPPED working one day and never returned again. I went back + forth between ASUS \ Best Buy and then forth + back again. Neither of them could figure out who was the right person to talk to at first. This occurred less than 1 year into owning this laptop. Best Buy said they couldn’t fix it, my warranty only covered getting it checked out in which I had to pack up the laptop (let’s remember that this is what I use for work and would be out of a laptop for up to a month or
more - this is what ASUS told me.) Asus also told me that I could upgrade my warranty, I said okay then would that cover a replacement so I could send in my current laptop and receive a new or refurbished one? And they said well actually none of our warranties cover replacement…… LOL okay, thanks for the suggestion then?! 
Never could send in my laptop before my warranty expired. Also, if you take it to any other repair shop even to just have it looked at - it could make your warranty nullified. I have troubleshooted for  countless hours and spent hours with ASUS support with no solution. They also said that even if I sent my laptop in, waited a month - 1.5 months and they couldn’t fix it that they’d just send it back as is…. This makes no sense to me. So I would risk shipping my laptop back and forth and potentially causing damage, be out of a device for work or borrow / buy something else in the meantime, for it possibly not even be fixed?? Literal nonsense. This was not even 1 yearrrrr after buying. 
2. When the second screen did work, it was cool and definitely great to have. However, it’s not easy to hold or position in your lap for drawing or artwork. It’s kind of awkward because the screens can only open to lay flat and they’re not actually even with one another. So, not the best but not a deal breaker totally. 
3. The ASUS pen that came with it is NOT good. There are also not a whole lot of options that compare to Apple Pencil IMO. 
4. Things that other people might care about (but don’t bother me really): fan is loud when running on full speed, no camera cover, gets really warm when in use and/or charging, a little bit on the heavy side, keyboard is super lightweight and feels flimsy tbh


Things that were great:
- The screen quality (when both worked + then when just one that works), super super clear and great color profiles 
- the battery life is actually really good in my opinion
- the amount and types of ports on the laptop are great (harder and harder to find laptops with a decent amount / types of ports these days) 
- runs a good amount of applications and systems at the same time without crashing out
- the stand that is attached is actually really great and I wish every laptop had this feature. So easy to view and switch from working at a desk to travel to whatever. 

Overall, would I recommend buying this laptop? Absolutely not. This laptop was just about as expensive as a Mac. I thought I was investing in something that would last a long time. Jokes on me I guess…
Do yourself a favor and skip all the research and grunt work and just go buy a Mac or something with high reliability and technical support and a good manufacturer warranty.

reviews.title: Strong laptop, just not the best fit for me
reviews.content:
This is a really cool and powerful laptop. The dual screens work well, and it is great for multitasking, schoolwork, and watching videos while working on something else. I also liked the way the keyboard attaches. The backlit keyboard feels good, and the built-in kickstand is a big plus because you do not need to carry an extra stand.

The main issue, in comparison, is the weight. Compared to the Lenovo Yoga Book 9i, this one feels heavier and not as easy to carry around for class or daily use. I used ot for a presentation and it did feel like carrying a similar sized gaming laptop.

I also noticed that when HDR was turned on, the screens looked dimmer, and the two screens did not seem to match in brightness. That may be a software issue, but it was noticeable. Turning it off fixed it but to me, why pay that much if its not working well.

Overall, this is a strong and well-built laptop. I would recommend it for someone who wants more power and likes the built-in stand design. It is not a bad devoce at all... 4.59 tops! For me, the Lenovo felt better for everyday use.

reviews.title: Great Laptop
reviews.content:
I don't normally write reviews, but wanted to share my experience since I was on the fence about this laptop. I bought it thinking it was probably going to be gimmicky, and I'd end up returning it after trying it for a couple days. I was very glad to be wrong -- it's got great screens, is very portable & not too heavy, has a good battery life despite the two screens, and never gets hot. I travel just about every other week, so I needed something that hit all three of those criteria, and this one definitely does. It also works great as a workstation when I'm home and just have it plugged into my external monitor. I've been impressed with the laptop.

I switched from a 16", and while I do wish sometimes the screen was bigger, I love how portable this is. I also tried the Lenovo Yoga Book (also dual screen monitor) -- the screens on that laptop were marginally better and I liked that you could fold it like a 2-in-1 (which you can't do with this one), but everything else about it was a lot worse (would get hotter & louder, hated the detached keyboard, etc.).

Also for context , most of my work is done in Citrix and Excel, so can't speak to any high-intensity use cases -- but this does very well for what I need.

The camera for some reason can only focus on one face and it makes the other face grainy even though its the same distance.

I think that the reason is that Best Buy wants customers to have to buy their warranty. I'm debating if I should return it just so I can get from a different seller so I have the 1 year warranty from Asus. Its a real bother though so I have been trying to talk to a manager but after waiting for an hour the line was cut. q_a.question: does it come with the pen? if not what is a compatible one?
q_a.answer: No, this laptop doesn't come with a Stylus pen. It is compatible with MPP 2.0 or 2.6, like the ASUS Pen 2.0 (SA203H) and ASUS Pen (SA205H), or third-party MPP 2.0 or MPP 2.0 Stylus pen.

q_a.question: I saw the storage was upgradable. What size M.2 is it? And does it fit dual sided or single sided only NVMEs?
q_a.answer: This ProArt PX13 (HN7306EA) laptop uses a compact M.2 2230 (22mm x 30mm) form factor for its NVMe PCIe 4.0 x4 SSD slot. It fits single-sided NVMe SSDs only due to surface-mounted components positioned close to the motherboard's M.2 slot, dual-sided SSDs will not have enough physical clearance and will not fit safely.

q_a.question: Can you add storage to this later on?
q_a.answer: Yes, you can upgrade the internal storage on this ProArt PX13 (HN7306EA) laptop by replacing the existing drive, but you cannot add a second drive because there is only one M.2 slot.

q_a.question: Is there a screen protector that doesn’t affect the touchscreen sensitivity
q_a.answer: Yes, there are ultra-thin plastic film screen protectors designed specifically for the ProArt PX13 laptop from third-party seller that maintain touchscreen sensitivity without hindering touch or stylus response.

q_a.question: Can It able to work with Linux distros like Fedora KDE, Kali Linux for network and cybersecurity?
q_a.answer: Yes, the ASUS ProArt PX13 (model HN7306EA) can work with Linux distributions like Fedora KDE and Kali Linux, but you will need a very new Linux kernel (v6.12 or newer) for proper hardware support.

q_a.question: How many external monitors can this laptop support?
q_a.answer: The ASUS ProArt PX13 (model HN7306EA) laptop can support up to three external monitors simultaneously, in addition to its built-in display. The laptop has two USB 4.0 Gen 3 Type-C ports that support display output and one HDMI 2.1 port for native monitor connections.

q_a.question: What is the Wattage (100% GPU/CPU) used total? Can it be charged using USB C?
q_a.answer: This specific laptop model has a combined CPU and GPU maximum thermal design power (TDP) of roughly 115 W to 120 W. Yes, the laptop can be charged using a USB-C charger. However, there are limitations, the USB-C port supports up to 100 W of Power Delivery (PD). If you are gaming or rendering videos at 100% capacity, a 100 W USB-C charger will not be able to fully run the laptop on maximum settings. During these heavy tasks, the system may occasionally dip into the battery for extra power. USB-C charger is perfect for charging while the laptop is in sleep mode.

q_a.question: Does this come with a pen? If not, what pens are compatible and where are they in stock at Best Buy stores?
q_a.answer: It works with my Microsoft Surface pen (but did not work with the Lenovo).

The only minor complaint I would have is the battery life will last about a days worth of classes and work give or take (charges fast though). Also, I wish the pen came with the laptop for a $2000 purchase but oh well. The 3K OLED looks amazing as well and it being touchscreen is something I also appreciate. Overall, I would give it 4.5 stars if I could.

reviews.title: Battery Life
reviews.content: I bought the ProArt PX13 for photo and video editing, and on performance it delivers — the OLED touchscreen is gorgeous and it handles my editing work with no lag. But three things keep it from being great. First, the battery life is poor; I'm looking for an outlet way sooner than I expected from a laptop at this price. Second, the SD card reader only takes the small microSD cards, so I need an adapter every time I want to load photos from my camera's full-size SD card. Third, for nearly $1,900, I expected more than 32GB of RAM and 512GB of storage — that fills up fast when you're working with photo and video files. If those things don't bother you, it's a powerful machine — but for a creator who's always on the go, they matter.

q_a.question: Why does this laptop feels like a vivobook?

The Zenbook chassis  is physically thinner and weighs less, whereas Vivobooks are typically heavier. q_a.question: Hey I've been researching this thing the best I can from what I've gathered it has the readeon 8060s which is entry level? everything i see compares it to the rtx 4070 thus the 4070 must be entry level or is amd claims of the igpu performance false?
q_a.answer:
Its an RDNA3.5 40CU iGPU with a relatively low TDP limit sharing up to 120W. It'll likely perform comparably to a desktop RX 7600 because of that. CPU wise, its effectively a TDP limited 9950x with quad channel 8000MT/sec RAM. Zen5 does great at low TDPs but still wants ~40W per CCD for optimal core clock boosting.

In this device specifically, it appears to have an 80W TDP limit which is about middle of the 45-120W range its capable of. That will be the limitation on the Max+ 395. Doesn't mean it won't perform amazingly, just more of a limitation than I was hoping as a USB4 eGPU host.

reviews.title: An Excellent Machine for Essentially Anyone
reviews.content:
As an average user that sometimes games and sometimes uses GIS software (which requires decent CPU power), this device absolutely slaughters everything I can throw at it. 

First off, the form factor for me is fairly perfect. It can fit into fairly small bags and has an extremely color accurate screen, with the 180 hz refresh rate it's extremely smooth. 
The CPU heavy tasks I throw at it are nothing, its as if the PC hums along without thinking, even on battery. I did spend some time allocating VRAM and understanding undervolting and things of that sort, which I know improves performance. 

As far as gaming, I havent found a game this thing can't run at good settings. I am always plugged in when gaming, since the one time I did game while on battery, it lasted about an hour. I think this thing works best on battery. 

Battery life does last quite a while on general tasks, I would say about 5 to 6 hours, but then on heavy tasks, I would just plug in because this thing will eat up your power. 

I think overall, this is a great machine, and definitely can fill multiple roles for many different people, but I would absolutely recommend it for pretty much anyone, because it should last you quite a while, and it's compact enough that you wont feel as though youre lugging around a gaming laptop.
