reviews.title: Great midrange gaming laptop pulls its own weight!
reviews.content:
This Acer Nitro V16 is a great midrange gaming laptop. It features an Intel Core 7 240H Series 2 (2024) processor, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 8GB VRAM GDDR7 dedicated video card, 16GB of RAM, expandable to 32GB, and a 512GB SSD with an extra slot to add another SSD if you chose to upgrade later. The laptop can handle some pretty fast paced high performance games. Let me break it all down. 

In the box comes the Acer Nitro V16 Gaming Laptop, Power Adapter and Cord, a Keychain, and paperwork. 

Setup is pretty simple for a laptop. There are basically two choices. One can set the laptop up from a backup or prior computer, or set it up as a new computer and not use any of the old settings. I opted to set it up as new. The process didn’t take that long. There were some pre-installed applications on the laptop that you may or may not want to keep. It wasn’t filled with a lot of junk like a lot of systems I have had. These are basic applications such as Dropbox, McAfee Antivirus, various Adobe applications, Xbox PC Gaming Pass for 3 months, and some proprietary software that Acer uses: NitroSense, and Acer’s Ai applications, which were pretty cool. I like the NitroSense because I can go there to look at my system performance and adjust settings like the different scenarios in which I would use the system, ie., Daily Use, Gaming, Quiet Occasion. The other settings in NitroSense are where the CPU, GPU and fan can be set to particular settings accordingly. 

Build and Design: The Acer Nitro V16 has a modern look and feel to it. It looks like it’s made for gaming with the 4 zone RGB backlit keyboard which also features a number pad. I love that it has a number pad. My last laptop didn’t have it and I missed it terribly. The chassis is built well and it looks pretty solid.

Display: This Acer Nitro V16 comes equipped with a 16” LCD screen that uses IPS technology. The colors are pretty accurate, but they aren’t very vivid. It’s good enough for gaming and daily use. It is even good for watching movies and videos. The colors could just be a bit more vibrant. The resolution is WUXGA at 1920 x 1200, so the picture is clear and detailed. I got smooth motion even when playing my fast paced games, due to the refresh rate of 165Hz. I was also able to see everything pretty good even in bright light because of the 400 nits brightness. In the NitroSense application, the option is there to turn on Acer Blue Light Shield to help protect your eyes. I do this when I will be doing a lot of productivity and reading on my laptop. 

Ports and connectivity are plentiful on this laptop. The ports are the power port, Ethernet, HDMI, USB, and Thunderbolt on the left side. On the right side of the laptop there are Kensington lock slot, 2 USB, 3.5mm headphone jack. Connectivity includes WiFi 6, Bluetooth, and Ethernet. 

Cooling and thermal performance has been great. Granted the fan gets it time in, and runs a lot during extended gaming sessions, but it gladly does its job. It can get a tad bit noisy, but only if you are sitting quietly with the sound off. I always have something playing: music, game audio, television, in game chats, etc., so it’s never quiet. I wasn’t bothered by the sound of the fan. Nonetheless, the system, during all of my extended gaming sessions, has remained cool and has never overheated. 

Summary: I really like this gaming laptop. The display leaves a little to be desired, but it’s not all that bad. I do like more RAM in my gaming laptops and I also like more storage. Luckily, this laptop has room to expand both the RAM, by replacing the two 8GB chips with 2 16GB chips, and to add an additional SSD in the empty slot. The laptop has good features and looks great. The Acer Nitro V16 is a great midrange gaming laptop that pulls its own weight!

reviews.title: Great Gaming Laptop
reviews.content:
The Acer Nitro V 16 has completely exceeded my expectations and offers an incredible balance of gaming performance, everyday productivity, and overall value. From the moment I powered it on, everything felt fast and responsive. The Obsidian Black finish gives the laptop a sleek, understated gaming look that is stylish without being overly flashy, making it just as comfortable in a classroom or office as it is in a gaming setup.

The 16-inch WUXGA display with its 165Hz refresh rate is one of the biggest highlights. Gameplay looks incredibly smooth, and the higher refresh rate makes a noticeable difference in fast-paced games. The colors are vibrant, the image is sharp, and the larger 16-inch screen provides plenty of space for gaming, streaming, and multitasking. Whether I'm playing competitive shooters, RPGs, or watching movies, the display consistently delivers an excellent viewing experience.

Performance has been outstanding thanks to the Intel Core 7 240H processor paired with the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 graphics card. Modern games run smoothly with impressive frame rates, and the laptop also handles video editing, photo editing, programming, and multitasking with ease. The 16GB of RAM keeps everything running smoothly even with multiple applications open, while the 512GB SSD provides fast boot times, quick game loading, and responsive application performance.

Cooling has also impressed me. Even during longer gaming sessions, the system stays relatively cool, and the fans do a great job keeping temperatures under control without becoming overly distracting. The keyboard feels comfortable for both gaming and typing, with responsive keys that make long sessions enjoyable.

I also appreciate the generous selection of ports, making it easy to connect an external monitor, gaming mouse, headset, or additional storage without needing extra adapters. The Wi-Fi connection has remained stable, and overall build quality feels solid and durable.

For anyone looking for a gaming laptop that delivers strong performance without breaking the bank, the Acer Nitro V is an excellent choice. It combines a beautiful high-refresh display, capable hardware, fast storage, and dependable performance into one well-designed package. Whether you're gaming, creating content, or simply need a powerful everyday laptop, this system offers outstanding value and is easy to recommend.

reviews.title: Fabulous Portable Gaming PC
reviews.content:
The Acer - Nitro V is a fabulous choice for someone who is looking for a portable gaming PC that is affordable, yet still is capable of playing most current and former PC games with ease. There are obviously performance limitations that need to be considered, but overall this gaming PC performs fabulously for its intended purpose. If you need a gaming PC that you can take on the go, it is an excellent choice. If you are space limited at home, it is also an excellent choice. 

The primary reason to choose a 14-inch gaming laptop is portability. It is in keeping with this consideration that I am rating this offering from ASUS. Without a doubt the ASUS ROG Zephyrus 14 fulfills this role by providing powerful gaming performance, coupled with maximum portability.

The Acer - Nitro V is slightly bulkier than most typical laptops. But it is thinner than most gaming laptops, so it occupies a happy medium. It has a nice assortment of ports to include a proprietary power port for the included power adapter. There is an USB-C PD port but it will not receive enough power to run this laptop without the battery draining down at the higher performance levels. As other reviewers have noticed, at the highest PC performance level the included brick adapter will not provide enough power to keep the battery from being run down. This is not a problem for me because I usually game at medium performance levels because I find that this provides the most stable and enjoyable game play.

The fan is noticeably loud but this does not surprise me. Putting powerful GPU and CPU components in such a small chassis will generate substantial heat. The only way to counteract the heat so the components don’t melt, is to engage a powerful fan.

The CPU and GPU specs are substantial and provide more than enough horsepower for PC gaming. I like to bring a gaming PC with me when I travel. So if I am trapped at an airport or otherwise have down time because I am delayed, I can get some gaming in. This device will be perfect for that purpose. Since I usually play a mobile game like Raids Shadow Legends on my phone when this happens, I decided to download it to this device. I am very familiar with the game and immediately noticed the improved performance and graphics. I am very much looking forward to using this laptop to get in some quick gaming when I travel. This type of game is perfect for times when you are running off of battery power because the processing draw is minimal.

The display is nice and functional. I prefer my gaming monitors when available, but the integrated display gets the job done nicely. The 16 inch display side provides excellent picture presentation and I think is an ideal size for portable gaming if you can manage the slightly larger footprint. 

The battery power is of course a limitation. When gaming on the battery I was able to get 3-4 hours, depending on the game. With Raids I was able to get substantially more time. There is a MUX switch and I recommend using it when on battery power if possible. This will have you gaming at lower performance levels but will maximize the battery time.When PC gaming on battery power, game dependent, I was able to get 3 or 4 hours of gameplay, with the NVIDIA GPU. Using the discrete GPU for standard computing tasks (web browsing, checking email, watching videos) I was able to get closer to 10 hours of use.

Since I don’t have as much time to game at home as I would like, the Acer - Nitro V gaming PC is going to make my frequent work and personal trips more enjoyable. Airport and weather delays are so frequent now that I am looking forward to using this laptop to help me pass the time. It is also a great companion to bring to a coffee shop and relax and game solo or with friends. Battery life is a consideration when a power plug is not available, but engaging the MUX switch makes a substantial difference.

reviews.title: Midrange Gaming, Top-Range Price
reviews.content:
The value-oriented brand with roots stretching back to eMachines has become something of a juggernaut as of late. Having absorbed former major players in the PC market including Packard Bell and Gateway, Acer’s computer offerings now extend all across the price gamut and even into peripherals. The Nitro gaming line has been around a while, with iterative updates every year to keep pace with newer specs. This Nitro 16 inch laptop packs a decent midrange punch and does well to keep cool, but a major sticking point leaves me wanting much more than what’s here.

- Unboxing and Setup
The Acer Nitro 16 unboxes in as just about a no-frills manner as you could expect. The spartan box contains only the laptop, power brick, a couple sparse pieces of warranty and health information, but Acer does include a Nitro keychain as a neat little pack-in. Otherwise, the setup and tutorial experience is on-device, and the standard Windows 11 setup process is straightforward with only a single Acer-specific addition for device registration if you desire. I’m also pleased to report that as of this review, workarounds for setting up Windows 11 without a Microsoft account are still possible.

While I’m grateful to see only a small amount of bloatware on the Nitro 16, there’s still some unwanted promotions, questionable Acer pack-ins (including an AI agent that nobody asked for)  and the notorious McAfee to deal with right off the bat.

The Nitro 16 is a surprisingly slim device for the hardware and port selection afforded. Three USB-A 3.2 ports are virtually unheard of nowadays, though more than one USB-C port would have been nice. Thankfully it’s a fully-featured Thunderbolt 4 port that supports Power Delivery for an alternate charging and power method besides the bulky AC adapter and the DC barrel jack. A 3.5mm combination microphone and headphone jack is a welcome sight, and the full size HDMI port makes connecting to external monitors a breeze. And love of all things, a proper full size Ethernet port backed up with a Killer NIC (though only Gigabit speeds) complements WiFi 6 and Bluetooth 5.3 connectivity.

- Performance
Equipped with a 10-core, 16-thread Intel Core Ultra 7 CPU and an 8GB Nvidia RTX 5060 mobile GPU, this configuration of the Nitro 16 is fairly capable at its default “Performance” profile. Loading up my go-to benchmark of Forza Horizon 6 with the “High + Ray Tracing” preset at the screen’s native 1920x1200 resolution, with no resolution scaling and the factory NVidia driver (January 2026), the benchmark achieved a very consistent 53 FPS with 1% lows just above 50. In-game performance at these settings held above 60FPS at all times, usually at or just above 70.

Unfortunately higher presets were pushing up against VRAM limitations and performance fell off a cliff - running the Extreme + Ray Tracing preset, the game became a 12-13 frame per second slideshow.

For those who want to game on battery or just enjoy a quieter-running laptop (on the Nitro’s Performance profile, both fans were spinning at moderate speed and were a clip louder than I’d like), the Balanced profile dropped performance by about 40%. Running the same benchmark and settings above, framerates hovered in the low to mid 30s and the fans were nearly silent.

Oddly enough, the run data showed that the GPU wasn’t limiting performance on the Balanced profile…GPU render was at 40-45 frames per second, but CPU performance was the bottleneck, with such a drastic fall-off that a single stutter was observed. I wouldn’t be surprised to see a future BIOS update boost the CPU’s performance in lower-power modes as it does appear to be more starved from the power budget than it should be. Even a two-watt adjustment could do wonders if it lets the high performance cores of the CPU run more freely.

- Screen, Sound, and Thermals
While it seems odd to go with a lower-resolution panel on a gaming laptop, the 1920x1200 16-inch panel is an IPS instead of the more common VA panel you’ll find on similar machines, and at 165Hz with adaptive sync the display is perfect for maxing out the RTX 5060. I found the high refresh rate made games running at lower framerates far less juddery than on a 60Hz display, and the panel delivers good color reproduction and depth with a decent, albeit not exceptional, vibrancy and brightness. At 400 nits the IPS display technically meets HDR400 specification, but HDR content on this display is only marginally more vivid than SDR.

As is par for course with most laptops, gaming or not, the built-in speakers are mediocre at best. In this machine they at least don’t sound terribly tinny, but they also don’t get particularly loud and can easily be drowned out by the cooling fans at full bore. Thankfully the 3.5mm headphone jack provides good audio quality with a clean DAC that seems to be well-suited for medium impedance headphones, and there are of course the USB ports and Bluetooth for alternate audio connections. As always, the laptop’s speakers are very much an “in a pinch” type beat.

Thermal management on the Nitro 16 is quite good. In its Balanced performance profile, I was able to go through an hour-long gaming session without the fans ramping up (they were virtually inaudible over the aforementioned weak speakers) while both GPU and CPU maintained about 75C. The Performance profile held around 80C while maxing both out, at the expense of fan noise that was significantly louder than most gaming laptops I’ve used as of late as both fans were on a high duty cycle the entire time. Turbo, the profile above Performance, was equally heavy on the fans but yielded temperatures at or above 90C for nearly indistinguishable FPS gains over Performance.

- Nitrosense and Battery Life
Acer includes the Nitrosense system management application as the primary way to change device settings, including the current power profile, 4-zone RGB lighting on the keyboard, color profiles for the screen, and more. The application is surprisingly easy to use with helpful descriptions and tool tips for each setting, and looks quite nice to boot. Most of my time spent in the app was changing power settings and the function of the power mode key at the top-left of the keyboard, setting it as a toggle between each of the four default power profiles: Eco (low CPU state, integrated graphics only), Balanced (standard CPU state, low GPU state), Performance (full CPU+GPU state), and Turbo (both overclocked).

Of note, only Eco and Balanced are available while the Nitro 16 is running on battery power or USB-C power delivery charging. The AC adapter is required to use Performance or Turbo.

As is typical with a gaming laptop, don’t expect long battery life for gaming. From a full charge on the Balanced profile with the screen at half brightness, I used up 25% of the battery in just over 20 minutes, suggesting the battery will last around an hour and a half at full bore. The news is much better when using the Eco profile and doing general tasks; when streaming a 93 minute movie the battery fell from 74% to 58%, estimating over 9 hours total battery life from full. Of course, your mileage may vary greatly depending on use case, power mode, and background software.

- Upgradeability, Build Quality
The Acer Nitro 16 is one of the more serviceable laptops I’ve seen in recent memory. The bottom side of the case is held in with just 9 screws, and with the panel off you have immediate access to the primary M.2 drive, an unpopulated secondary M.2 slot, the two SODIMM DDR5 memory modules, and the WiFi & Bluetooth module on a mini PCIe connector. The battery can be replaced, the CPU & GPU heatsink is a standard design with replaceable fans, and the mainboard can be swapped out if needed.

Overall the Nitro 16 has passable design and build. Plastics are standard midrange laptop fare, and there’s just enough flex in the keyboard tray when typing to remind you of that fact. The keyboard keys do feel quite nice under the fingertips, using higher quality chiclet-style keys and rubber domes than usual. The generously oversized trackpad feels fine and tracks well. The lid and screen are fairly rigid and don’t twist any concerning amount.

One area that could be an issue for long term ownership is the hinge. The lid has much less resistance to angle adjustments than other 15 and 16 inch laptops I’ve used, to the point where gravity or air can close the lid from shallow angles, and it exhibits a bit of wobble. This appears to be due to a simplified (cost-cutting?) hinge design that only connects one side of each hinge to the laptop base, and they’re fairly narrow at that. As these are the highest-stress points on a laptop I would take extra care to monitor these through the warranty period for signs of premature wear or failure.

- Bottom Line
The most noteworthy thing about the Nitro 16 is that I didn’t note the one issue I have with most other gaming laptops…it doesn’t get concerningly hot nor does it overheat. While I have my reservations about its build quality and longevity, it does a phenomenal job delivering its power, and overall seems no worse for it than any other midrange gaming laptop. This would be a solid choice amongst its peers.

But, it’s time to address the elephant in the room. With an MSRP pushing nearly two thousand dollars, even rotating sales bringing this machine down to the low-thousands doesn’t make up for the fact that only 16GB RAM and a 512GB SSD is a pitifully minimal spec, even in the AI-demand driven market that’s pushing RAM and NAND prices sky-high as of this review’s posting. The RAM I can understand, but 512GB is pitiful when modern AAA games can push over 150GB installed.

Take a little more time to shop and compare because while you can always upgrade these things after purchase, it’s an awful high cost of entry to get weak specifications today, and the overall quality doesn’t make up the price gap. Grab it on a deep discount; otherwise, not recommended.

reviews.title: A stealth, hybrid laptop. Powerful indeed.
reviews.content:
The Acer Nitro V16 is a slim gaming laptop featuring a combination of the Intel Core 7 240H and the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060. The best way to describe it is a hybrid powerhouse designed to blur the line between a dedicated gaming rig and a sharp, professional daily driver, offering remarkably balanced hardware at a relatively accessible entry price. It promises modern graphical capabilities without the excessive weight usually tied to the category.

It is highly portable despite the 16-inch screen, proving lighter than expected and easy to carry for a daily commute. The RTX 5060 does well handling the majority of games, and it performs excellently with design and simulation software. Dedicated GPU power is increasingly necessary for both modern daily work and gaming applications. The 16GB RAMs are just fine. I usually like them at a higher number. This Acer is doing just fine.

Acer delivers a remarkable look with the sleek aesthetic, making the machine subtle enough for a classroom, office, or professional environment. It offers full customization to adapt to your tasks, including fan speed adjustments and keyboard lighting via software. The camera features a built-in physical privacy lock, a feature that should ideally be implemented on all modern laptops.

The cooling fans and heatsink maintain relatively low temperatures during standard use, though the system can run hot when pushed to its absolute limit. Battery life is not a strong suit for portability, lasting roughly 2.5 hours on mixed usage, which is typical for this category. However, the included power adapter is highly capable and charges the laptop in a very short time.

Connectivity ports are somewhat sparse, featuring only one USB-C port, but it does include a full HDMI port and an RJ-45 Ethernet port (Thunderbolt). The integrated webcam is a standard 720p model. It provides a slightly soft image that naturally softens background details during video conferences, which can be preferable to high-definition alternatives. Audio performance is underwhelming; the downward-firing speakers get loud but lack bass. Because most users rely on headphones for gaming, this is less of an issue, and the quality remains perfectly adequate for basic notifications and casual videos.

This laptop is highly recommended for anyone looking for a powerful machine to run heavy simulations or engineering design applications. It handles intensive workloads efficiently while remaining fully capable of running modern games or serving as an occasional gaming getaway on its large, high-resolution 16-inch screen.

reviews.title: A reasonable offering for 2026
reviews.content:
It's a strange and difficult time to purchase anything gaming related, be it a PC or even the rapidly rising prices of 5 year old consoles. This laptop is a testament to that, offering a processor that came out in 2024 with only 16gb of ram and 512gb of SSD storage.

It offers a RTX5060 with 8gb of ram, which means you really wont be able to take much advantage of things like Ray tracing or ultra high resolution textures, but will offer smooth performance in most games using frame gen. The 50 series supports multi-frame generation and dynamic multi-frame generation, the current latest and greatest from Nvidia, but you'll need to be plugged into the wall. The intel 240h is a 10 core processor, 6 p-cores (with hyperthreading) and 4 e-cores that will suck up to 115W max which is actually more than the GPU. With a 76Wh battery your battery life away from the plug isn't going to be very long. When plugged you'll be able to play the majority of games at reasonable settings other than some of the latest and greatest AAA games.

The rest of the hardware is adequate, the keyboard has nice travel on the keys and a good actuation weight. Features a fairly large trackpad, and being a 16" it has as number pad as part of the keyboard layout. The 16" screen is a IPS panel with a 16:10 aspect ratio which is nice for those also using this for productivity tasks or content creation, offering 1920x1200 resolution and a respectable 165hz refresh rate. The screen hinge is incredibly light, easy to open with one finger, but will easily flop around if you try to move it while open or jiggle depending on your typing surface.

Lots of connectivity by todays standards, 3x USB A, a USB C with 10gbps capability, a HDMI port, a headphone jack, a gigabit ethernet port, and to my dismay features a charger that uses a banana plug. The decision to use a banana plug for the charge is odd to me, the charger is 135 which is achievable over a USB C connection but they opted not to.

Acer didn't include as much bloatware as some other manufactures do these days, but still includes some Acer AI app, Acer Nitro app, McAfee, a Dropbox promotion, and a few other piece of bloatware. Its pretty easy to be sitting at 50% ram usage in windows just browsing the web, so definitely some optimization that can be done mostly by removing all that junk.

Sadly this is the reality of PC hardware currently, and it won't be correcting itself anytime soon most are expecting these inflated prices to last at least until 2028. If you are shopping in this price range you should certainly consider this laptop but overall a bit disappointing due to the inflated cost of components currently.

reviews.title: Good Budget Gaming Laptop
reviews.content:
The Nitro V 16 is a good entry-level gaming laptop and a pretty good value even as RAM and storage prices continue to get out of control. It’s not perfect, but it’s great for 1080p gaming and the cuts made are mostly sensible. My only problems are the slightly mediocre display and that the included charger is not capable of powering this laptop in its highest performance mode. I do think this is worth considering though, especially if it goes on sale.

The Nitro V 16 has an understated look with a few subtle accents and doesn’t look too gaudy or gamer-y. It’s also relatively thin and light for a gaming laptop and easy to travel with. It’s an all plastic build, but the build quality is excellent with very little flex and no creaking or cheap-feeling parts. The screen can fold all the way back to 180 degrees and stays in place.

For specs, you are getting an RTX 5060 GPU with 8GB of GDDR7 at 75W. 75W is about the middle of the RTX 5060’s power range, so this is not the most powerful RTX 5060 GPU available in terms of pure wattage. The Intel Core 7 240H is a decent CPU with 6 performance cores and 4 efficiency cores, though contrary to its Series 2 designation it’s actually based on the previous generation Raptor Lake architecture. 16GB of DDR5-5600 is provided via 2 SODIMM modules and this can be upgraded. The 512GB Gen 4 SSD is quite fast at 7500 MB/s read and 5500 MB/s write, though this will fill up quickly with how big modern PC games are and will need to be managed. There is an additional NVMe slot on the mainboard, so more storage can be added later. Opening the laptop is very easy and involves removing 9 exposed philips head screws.

On the left side of the laptop there is the proprietary charging port, Ethernet, HDMI 2.1, USB-A 10Gbps, and a USB-C Thunderbolt 4 (also capable of charging). On the right side there are (2) 5Gbps USB-A ports and a headphone/microphone jack. It’s a good selection of ports, though I would personally swap one of the USB-A ports for another USB-C.

The display is a 1920x1200 IPS LCD with a 165Hz refresh rate. As far as laptop displays go it is okay but not the best. Colors look washed out compared to higher-end laptop displays I’ve seen. According to Acer’s website it covers 45% of the NTSC color gamut, which is well short of 100% sRGB. For gaming I’d say it does look good in most games and the 165Hz refresh rate looks great when that framerate can be achieved, but if you have a usage that depends on accurate color reproduction this probably isn’t the one. This does seem like a downgrade compared to previous versions of the Nitro V that used a 180Hz screen that did hit very close to 100% sRGB.

The Windows 11 install has a little bit of bloat - some unnecessary Acer programs, McAfee Antivirus, and a few advertisements in the start menu, but they were easy enough to remove. The NitroSense app lets you change the laptop-specific settings, including the performance mode and works well enough. The app can be ignored for the most part once you have your preferences dialed in, which is a good thing.

At 1080p, I’d generally class the performance as similar or slightly better at equivalent settings to a PS5 or Xbox Series X, with the added benefit of DLSS upscaling. I can run Alan Wake 2 on the Medium preset at 1920x1200 with DLAA and get around 40fps in the heaviest forest sections of the game. I can also hit 60fps comfortably on Forza Horizon 6 at the High preset with DLAA as well. Plugging into an external display, 1440p is possible with some settings adjustments and upscaling, but 4K seems just out of reach for modern games, even at very low settings. This is all using the Performance power setting in NitroSense. Turbo gives you about 8-10% more performance, but it comes at the cost of battery drain, even when plugged in, so I’d consider that a no-go in general.

The Nitro V 16 includes a 135W charger with a right angle barrel connector. At this wattage it would have been nice to see 140W USB-C charging, but I can forgive that in a budget gaming laptop. The USB-C port does support charging but only up to 100W. The charging brick and AC cord combined give you about 10ft of length from the outlet. The downfall of the charger is that it is not capable of keeping the laptop charged at its highest performance mode (Turbo) and the battery drains in this mode under load. It means that, even while plugged in, you are only going to get maybe a few hours of use in the highest performance mode before it has to drop down. The second highest performance mode (Performance) did not drain in my testing, so I’d consider this the default when plugged in.

The fans can get pretty loud in Turbo mode, but in Performance mode they don’t generally disrupt the experience or anyone around you. A good pair of headphones should shut out most of the fan noise either way.

The keyboard and trackpad are both very good. I do have a small issue with the keyboard where the right shift key is a little smaller to make room for the arrow keys and I sometimes will hit one of them accidentally while typing, but overall it’s good. You get a numpad as well, which I always appreciate on a bigger laptop. The key travel feels about right and the 4-zone RGB backlight covers all the keys evenly. The trackpad is a good size and offers all the standard multitouch capabilities. It has a nice click to it as well.

Battery life feels about average for gaming a laptop. In the Eco performance mode, it seems to land at around 4-6 hours or so depending on what I am doing. I wouldn’t feel comfortable leaving the charger at home, but it should get through a good chunk of the day before needing to be plugged in. The other available mode on Battery is Balanced and this drops the battery life significantly compared to Eco.

Wireless connectivity includes Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.2. Wi-Fi 6 is an older standard at this point, but I was still able to pull down about 700 Mbps on my Gigabit internet connection at about 15ft from my router.

The built-in webcam is 1080p 30fps. The quality is okay. There is no Windows Hello functionality for face unlock here. It does have a physical privacy shutter though.

The speakers are okay, but not great. They’re clear and loud enough for voice, but most other content sounds tinny and compressed. As with the fans though a decent pair of headphones will solve this problem.

I think the Acer Nitro V 16 is a very good budget gaming laptop if you can find it for the right price, especially if you are just getting into PC gaming and don’t have the space for a permanent setup. The display is a bit of a letdown and the battery drains at the highest performance mode, but overall what it has to offer is compelling.

reviews.title: It will surprise you in performance
reviews.content:
PROS:

* It will run a lot of great games on Ultra settings (The Last of Us Part 1, The Witcher 3)
* The UI is snappy and quick
* Fan noise isn’t obnoxious, even when it’s fighting for its life



SO-SO:

* The screen quality (It’s LED and matte, which brings down the colors)
* Build quality; materials used 



CONS:

* Price to spec ratio is extremely unbalanced (thanks to RAM prices)
* I’d like to see a free case, mouse, or other accessories added if the price is going to rise this much





It’s a rough time to get into PC gaming. We’ve all heard about RAM shortages, but prices have exploded across the industry. It’s a shame because for many, PC gaming isn’t possible when even less feature-heavy machines cost $1,500 or more. I hope things return to normal when the RAM shortage eases, but I don’t have high hopes since companies rarely lower prices.



With that out of the way, the new Acer Nitro WUXGA is a laptop that will satisfy your gaming itch. We ordered it as an entry-level machine for our son, who mainly plays on consoles. He was very excited, even though it lacks much of what I expect in a laptop. It has no OLED screen but an LED one that isn’t the best quality. The picture is great in the right lighting, but the matte screen feels muddy compared to what I’m used to. On the other hand, my son loves it.


While it may be hard to start PC gaming now due to prices, it’s a great time to explore games you haven’t played before at max settings. That’s what he’s doing. He’s playing The Witcher 3 and The Last of Us Part 1. Both run on Ultra settings on this machine, which surprised me. Not only are the settings maxed, but gameplay is smooth with no lag or unstable frame rates. It performs very well.



The fan kicks on during heavy on-screen action, but it isn’t as obnoxious as many low to mid-tier PCs. It performs better than I expected, given the screen quality. To my son, this may as well be a high-end $3500 machine, and that’s what matters to me.



I’d wait for prices if this is what $1600 gets you. Yes, my son doesn’t know better and loves playing on it, but as an older gamer, I find the price hard to swallow. In these cases, companies could offer free add-ons to reduce sticker shock, like a case, headphones, or a gaming mouse. They don’t have to be expensive but could show some grace toward consumers. After all, it’s not our fault there’s a shortage.

reviews.title: Good gaming laptop
reviews.content:
For 2026 this laptop should give you more for the price but considering the shortages of RAM and storage these days I guess it is what it is. I remember when you can get a nitro gaming laptop for under $1,000 and the specs wouldn't be so bad but between the shortages and inflation this is what we get. 

Specs:
165Hz 1080p+ display IPS
Intel Core 7 240H
16GB DDR5 Memory
Nividia 5060 8GB GDDR7 VRAM
512GB SSD

The computer is familiar if you have ever used an Acer Nitro laptop before in terms of the software suite and the keyboard goes. Nothing has really changed better or for worse. It has decent travel and it does the job. also has a multi zone RGB backlight. The laptop also is black and could easily fit in a office or school background without it looking out of place if you wanted to use it there was well. the 16GB of memory is fine enough but I wish it got more with how games are using more and more RAM but it will do fine enough for most games. I had no issues playing most games ive tried on this. Can't play games  at max settings but if you lower the settings this will do fine in 2026.

reviews.title: Excellent performance and premium build
reviews.content:
I’m extremely impressed with the MSI Stealth 16 AI. The OLED QHD+ 240Hz display is absolutely stunning — colors are vibrant, blacks are deep, and motion is incredibly smooth. It’s perfect for gaming, content creation, and everyday work.
The Intel Ultra 9 processor paired with the RTX 5070 delivers outstanding performance. Games run flawlessly at high settings, and multitasking is fast and effortless thanks to the 32GB of RAM. The 1TB SSD is very fast and provides plenty of storage.
Despite its power, the laptop stays relatively quiet and cool, and the slim, clean design makes it look professional rather than “flashy gaming.” The keyboard feels great, and overall build quality is premium.
This laptop strikes a perfect balance between power, portability, and design. Highly recommended for anyone looking for a high-end gaming or productivity laptop.

reviews.title: Simply an Amazing Experience
reviews.content: Upon opening the laptop you can immediately distinguish the premium weight and feel. I've used this laptop for approximetely 3 weeks now and has simply been the greatest gaming experience I've ever had (coming from console). The QD+ OLED panel make colors pop like no other monitor I've seen and with a 240hz refresh rate you will notice al.ost immidiate response times. i havent noticed any sort of rendering or laginess to my daily use. I've struggled to purchase but have always been intrigued by MSI. I am thankful i purchased there product becauae it is simply the most beautiful screen I've seen. The one down side of it is the glossy finish due to the QD+ technology so if you use this as a work/play area in a bright room some may be annoyed by the glare.

reviews.title: Good So Far
reviews.content: As I strictly use this laptop for gaming and sometimes to stream. So far, I am very satisfied with it. It runs better than my last MSI laptop that was a 4060 and had similar specs. It doesn't overheat as easily, and it had all the pros my previous gaming laptop had. I will note, that the display at times turns on and off as if it was refreshing, which I find strange. It happens completely unprompted as well. The battery life is excellent and I love the speed! Makes gaming very enjoyable with little to no lag.

reviews.title: Dell?! More like “Deal”!
reviews.content:
In a word, this Dell Laptop is a paradox.  It’s one of the smallest, big laptops I’ve had the opportunity to use.  It’s one of the lightest, but still robust laptops that I can attest to.  I do want to address a couple of the deficiencies first:

Lack of USB A and C on BOTH sides of the laptop- While I appreciate the fact that Dell does not use a proprietary charging system, but rather utilizes a USB interface, it would be nice if I had one on each side to decide on which side I can charge.  This is especially helpful if I were to plug into a dock and needed to use my screen.  If I only have one side to plug into, the screen may point the wrong way.

Lack of a Privacy Screen for Camera- This one is weird.  Because older models of Dells that I have used all have this option of a little, internal slide that manually covers the camera lens.  I can’t imagine this is much of a cost saver and would hope that all laptops would have this as an included feature.

I wish the backlit keyboard had a few more dimming options.  Nothing that would stop me from recommending this laptop, but one or two more dimmer settings would have been nice.

Now on to the good stuff!

That 16” screen!!! Man, do a few inches make a difference (hehe)! It is very noticeable when compared to the typical 13” - 15” screens.  And while it is larger, it does not carry the bulk of my previously large laptops.

With that added screen size comes additional room for the keyboard.  And having a full size keyboard with a numeric keypad is something that, at least for me, is a must.  While this computer will be used for streaming, emails, writing documents, etc., there will be a lot of times that numeric data entry will be accessed, and having that keypad is a gamechanger.  This is something that smaller laptops concede because of space.

With having a laptop this big, it feels like a desktop monitor, and as such I forget about the touchscreen all the time. Having not just a touchscreen, but a multi-touch screen is a huge win (when I remember :-) ).  The ability to go through forms and documents that contain check boxes and buttons makes this option a necessity.  Being able to zoom in on objects by using multi-touch to stretch the object is such a timesaver. Some screens have an odd feel to them, like my finger is dragging over them.  Not this laptop!  The screen is really responsive and because of that, paired with the tactile sensation of a smooth screen, it feels natural.

Although it has a HDMI 2.1 port, the better option for me is to use  one of the two Thunderbolt ports to plug into the computer dock.  This laptop will obviously work with a Dell Dock.  However, I know there are some third party docks out there that have better options.  I had a 3rd party Thunderbolt dock that worked seamlessly with this laptop.  Just do your research to make sure a 3rd party dock is compatible before purchase.  Either way, I had two additional screens hooked up to the dock.  The laptop handled it with ease.  Whether it was playing a movie on the laptop screen, while doing work on my other two monitors, or switching objects between monitors for quick editing and copying, I didn’t notice any lag.

While all of this is true, please do not confuse this laptop with being a capable gaming laptop.  It is NOT, and it wasn’t built to be.  This laptop is a fully capable, travel-ready companion that is able to give you many of the desktop features without the bulky size.

I would recommend this laptop to friends and family.

reviews.title: Great for gaming on the go
reviews.content:
The Acer Predator Neo Gaming Laptop packs a lot in its frame. The OLED 16” 2560x1600 @240Hz screen is backed by an Intel Core Ultra 9 Series 2, and Nvidia RTX 5070Ti mobile. It also comes with 16GB RAM, and a 1TB M.2 SSD. The core components give it enough space and power to run games at decent levels. With DSR you can get more frames or details out of the GPU. The price may be higher than expected, but the price of RAM needed for parts has gone through the roof. It has an HDMI port on the back with a power supply (custom barrel) and a USB port. USB-A and C ports also line the side of the unit. Fans blow the exhaust out of the back of the unit. For a gaming laptop it’s not too heavy at just under 5 pounds. A 2.5GB Ethernet port along with the latest Bluetooth and Wi-Fi give all the connectivity options you’ll need. The keyboard is backlit and you can customize the colors by region, or have them breathe, pulse etc. There is a numpad to the right side. The touchpad is a nice size and responsive, just off centered to the left of center. The dark gray colors look nice. The build is mostly plastic and has some flexing to it, but still feels solid. 
     The laptop comes with Windows Home 11. After bootup the bloatware is minimal. Third party is McAffee, but it’s easy to remove the two programs in Windows “add or remove” programs with a search. Acer has several programs from a monitor of the device, to a “AI” helper. Windows has co-pilot installed. There is also the Intel Killer software for making modifications for gaming and prioritizing traffic etc. Pick and choose what you want to keep or remove. After that, it’s a straightforward windows setup and adding programs you want. With the Ethernet I can get full 2.5GB/s with up to 280MB/s throughput. Wifi connected at AX on wifi 6, and did fine on 5GHz and 2.4 channels too. Speed should not be an issue in connecting to anything. The keyboard has a nice response feel and is not as crowded as other 16” monitor laptops. The numpad on the right is small, but at least it has one. The backlit colors come through fine and are easy to use in dark rooms. 
     For gaming this will get you in the mid-range of abilities with no issues. When I have the unit plugged in, I run in turbo mode. Makes more fan noise when gaming, but you’ll get more out of it. The laptop will also throw out a lot of heat by the back, and after a while the heat will come up through the keys. Won’t burn, but it is noticeable. Having good ventilation around and under the laptop will help. The screen looked great in gaming, colors and no tearing. You can choose between the onboard GPU or the discrete 5070 Ti. In the BIOS and the Nvidia options I just chose the Nvidia GPU to be used all the time. DSR can help with graphics if needed. The 5070 Ti comes with 12GB of RAM so it’s enough for at least mid-range graphic options. The 16GB of RAM will meet minimum specs for advanced games. The GPU HDMI port was also able to use a 5120x1440 monitor with no issues. I turned off the laptop screen when using a 2nd monitor. In 3D Mark, the laptop got 3650 in regular Steel Nomad, and 4180 in Speedway.
     Upgrades can be done. Taking the back of the laptop off, see pictures, uses torx heads, you can see room for another M.2. Also, I found the laptop can hold up to 32GB of DDR5 RAM. I used some RAM from my former laptop, upgraded the RAM and added an extra M.2 for more storage space. The first boot after adding RAM will take longer, but the machine used it fine. The 2nd M.2 showed up with no issues. 32GB of RAM did help in games and productivity. The 5070 Ti is about the same as 4080, and a solid mobile GPU. The CPU also does well with its P and E cores. The screen looks great. For gaming on the go, this is a great option. Good power, and not too heavy. It can get hot, so make sure you turn down the power level, or have good ventilation. I would take this with me on the road.

reviews.title: Slim, fast, and one upgrade from great
reviews.content:
Thin gaming laptops usually make you pick a side. Either it's light enough to carry and the hardware gets choked, or the hardware is serious and you're hauling a brick. Acer's Predator Helios Neo 16S lands closer to the middle than most. Inside you get a 24-core Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus, an RTX 5070 Ti with 12GB of VRAM, 16GB of DDR5, and a 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD, all in a chassis that's under three quarters of an inch thick and about 4.85 pounds. I split my time on it between gaming and regular work, and it handled both without much fuss.

That screen, though. It's a 16-inch 2560x1600 OLED at 240Hz, and it's easily one of the nicest panels I've used on a laptop. Blacks are actually black, colors pop without looking cartoonish, and motion stays crisp. Hard to go back after this.

Gaming is mostly fast multiplayer shooters for me, and this is where the 240Hz panel and the 5070 Ti pair up nicely. At native resolution with settings at high or maxed, things stayed smooth and responsive, and G-Sync kept tearing out of the picture. On the work side, the CPU barely broke a sweat. Browsers, office apps, and the usual pile of background stuff all felt snappy. For the competitive crowd, the 2.5G Ethernet port is a welcome touch, and the Killer Wi-Fi 6E held up fine when I wasn't wired in.

Push it on the Turbo profile and the fans get loud. No surprise there, and frankly it's what I'd expect from a machine this thin pushing this much hardware. You trade some quiet for sustained performance. I liked that Acer added a dedicated key to cycle power profiles, so jumping from Quiet for work to Turbo for a match is one press instead of a trip into settings. PredatorSense handles the rest, with temps, fan curves, and RGB all in one spot.

Here's my one real caveat. 16GB of RAM is tight for this tier. Running a demanding game with a few things open in the background, I could see memory getting maxed, and it's the bottleneck I'd want to fix first. The good news is that the memory is socketed, two 8GB sticks in two slots, so you can upgrade later without replacing the whole machine. If you know you multitask hard, though, look for a config that ships with 32GB from the start.

Build feels solid. Hinge is firm, the deck doesn't flex, and the full keyboard with a numpad is comfortable for both games and long typing sessions. I mostly kept it plugged in, which is how I'd treat any gaming laptop, so battery life wasn't a factor for me. Acer throws in a padded sleeve, and the 230W brick is reasonably compact for what it powers.

So should you buy it? If you want a gaming laptop that's thin enough to carry daily, has a gorgeous OLED panel, and has the horsepower for competitive shooters at high settings, this is an easy one to recommend. Just plan on more RAM, either now with a bigger config or as an upgrade down the road.

reviews.title: A Must Have!!!
reviews.content:
I’ve been really impressed with the Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI so far. It has an RTX 5070 Ti, Intel Core i9 processor, and 16GB of RAM, so there’s plenty of power for gaming, school, work, and everyday use.
The 16 inch 16:10 OLED display is probably one of my favorite things about this laptop. The screen looks amazing, with great colors and deep blacks, and the 16:10 aspect ratio gives you a little more vertical screen space for schoolwork and browsing. Since the laptop is fairly thin for a gaming laptop, it’s also pretty easy to carry around, which is a big plus if you’re using it for school or work.
Gaming performance has been great. I tested Cyberpunk 2077 at medium settings with ray tracing enabled and was getting around 50–70 FPS with DLSS set to Performance and frame generation turned off. For newer games, the performance is more than enough for playing at medium to high settings.
The 1TB of storage is also nice because you have plenty of room for games and other files. If you need more storage, the built-in microSD card slot makes it easy to add extra space.
I also really like the PredatorSense app. It gives you an easy way to keep an eye on temperatures and switch between different performance modes like Quiet, Balanced, Performance, and Turbo. Turbo mode is especially useful when the laptop is plugged into AC power and you want to get the most performance possible.
There are a couple of things I don’t love, though. The laptop can get pretty hot, even when I’m just browsing the web or doing schoolwork. That’s something to be aware of if you’re going to be using it for long periods. I also think it’s a little strange that the USB-C ports are located on the back. Since USB-C is something I use pretty often, having those ports on the rear isn’t always the most convenient.
A nice bonus is that Acer includes a laptop cover, which makes carrying the laptop around easier and gives it a little extra protection.
Overall, I’m very happy with this laptop. You get a lot of performance for the price, the OLED screen looks fantastic, and it’s thin enough to be practical for carrying to school or work. The heat and rear USB-C ports are my main complaints, but neither takes away from how good the laptop is overall. If you’re looking for a powerful gaming laptop that can also work well for school and everyday use, this is definitely worth considering.

reviews.title: Too thin to be this fast?
reviews.content:
Pros:
Gorgeous Display
Excellent build quality
Lightweight for a gaming laptop
Probably the thinnest gaming laptop I’ve owned so far
Superior cooling system. So far, it has not run extremely hot like my previous gaming laptop, where the temps would stay around the mid to high 90s.

Cons:
Speakers are not great; they sound loud and tinny. Headphones are a must, especially when the fans kick into overdrive to keep this monster cooled.
Software hiccups during setup and afterwards. This could be due to restoring from my previous laptop; a factory reset and setup as a new device cleared most of the bugs.
Random audio crackling that is software-related, not hardware. It’s less noticeable when using Bluetooth headphones.
Display is stuck on 240Hz with no option to lower it down at all.
Battery life is on the lower side. Using the quiet profile and keeping brightness around 50%, I managed to get 4 hours of battery life with just web browsing and streaming media.

Resident Evil 4:
Max settings at display resolution
FPS: 87–110 (drops only during demanding scenes)
Temps hover around the mid-70s but never cross 80°C. Even with the GPU pulling 100W+ and utilization almost at 100%, and the CPU around 40–50W, it managed to keep temperatures under 80°C.
Drops to the low 60s with a laptop cooling pad.
Profile set to Turbo.

Grid Legends, Forza Motorsport, and the latest Forza Horizon titles ran similarly—temperatures were kept under control and delivered high FPS with high settings.

Basically, the Neo 16s has plenty of power for AAA games. With how efficient the latest Intel chips and Nvidia GPUs are, it translates to better performance at lower wattage compared to previous generations. It has strong hardware that produces beautiful visuals for this gorgeous OLED display, making it a joy to use for gaming, consuming content, and day-to-day tasks. Note that it is a glossy panel, so outdoor usage will be a struggle.

The 16GB of RAM is plenty for gaming and basic tasks like having multiple tabs and a few applications open. If you’re the type of person who has 100 tabs open and also wants to stream gameplay, I recommend the 32GB model. With how much PC hardware prices have risen, it’s cheaper to buy that model upfront than upgrading it afterwards. It comes with a pair of 8GB sticks, so the only option to upgrade to 32GB would require purchasing a pair of 16GB RAM sticks. You can buy a single 16GB stick, but it will only run in dual-channel up to 8GB since it isn't a matching pair.

Overall, I’m very happy with the Neo 16s. It’s impressive hardware that manages to be lightweight and thin for a 16-inch gaming laptop. It’s a shame that recent price hikes have forced PC manufacturers to cut back on storage or RAM size to keep prices from getting out of hand. It’s pricey, but in return—aside from the base RAM size—you get powerful hardware, especially on the GPU and CPU sides. The build quality is excellent, and the display is top-notch. For most people, 16GB of RAM will be plenty; if you’re a power user who tends to have a lot of things open or streams gameplay, I would steer you to the 32GB model. For everyone else, this OLED machine punches way above its weight class and handles heavy gaming workloads with ease.

reviews.title: This Predator Is Your Ally!
reviews.content:
Acer Preadtor Helios NEO 16s AI

Looks: 

Simple, more elegant execution of the masculine gaming laptop aesthetic. It's still true to what it is; Matte black with subtle nods to what beastly hardware might be under the hood, but you won't feel self conscious or embarrassed using it out in public. Set the RGB backlighting to a solid color like white, and it'll blend right in with other professional laptops.

Build quality: 

Solid build. Hinge is smooth, stable, not too tight. Everything feels premium to the touch. Like all matte finish surfaces, it's a fingerprint magnet.

Keyboard: 

It's a full keyboard. Which means a full suite of dedicated media keys, a number-pad, and a couple of unique keys, which is very nice to have. Pleasant to type on. Keys feel satisfying to press and responsive while remaining very quiet. Fully backlit with addressable RGB software. The track-pad is adequate. 

Screen: 

The screen is gorgeous. Best I've seen on a laptop. 2560x1600 240Hz refresh rate OLED with G-Sync is gonna be hard to beat in this space. The screen is a little reflective in the light simply due to the nature of the panel. Colors really pop and blacks are deep which is what you'd expect from an OLED panel. The VESA HDR certification ensures you're able to take advantage of HDR compatible content. Though this true black 500 Certification is on the lower end of VESA certifications, it's still far superior to even the best LCD screen and is very impressive to find in a laptop form factor. Th 240Hz refresh rate is buttery smooth while gaming, modeling in fusion 360, or normal use. The G-Sync ensures there's no screen tearing while gaming. Just overall a very pleasing to the eye screen- excellent execution. 

Hardware Specs: 

It's fast. It's powerful. The RTX 5070ti in this is an absolute weapon. 12Gb of VRAM on top of the system's 16gb of RAM really helps with rendering and cutting down on loading times. Paired up with the Intel Core Ultra 9 CPU, this thing can play games at impressive graphical settings. 3D modeling in fusion 360, was a cake walk. It will chew through most everything the average enthusiast will probably throw at it. One caveat: like all gaming designated laptops, this thing runs HOT when under load. The fans work very well at helping to shed the heat and protect the internals, but that means it's shedding the heat potentially onto YOU, so doing demanding tasks while it's sitting in your lap is not recommended. Keep it up on a hard surface so it can adequately shed the heat. This is simply the nature of the beast when it comes to high performance laptops, though. 

Gaming Performance:  

The suite of games I used to test this were: Forza Horizon 5, Cyberpunk 2077, and Monster Hunter Wilds.

It easily chewed through Forza Horizon 5; no surprise there. Max settings, high stable frame-rates. Performed masterfully, as expected. Cyberpunk was a much tougher beast, no surprises there. Had to play with some things on medium and only taking advantage of certain ray tracing and real shadows/ reflections features. The game still looks gorgeous and is very playable at these high settings, but it's still part tech demo so it's gonna stress test any hardware. This machine performed very admirably, especially given the portable form factor. Monster Hunter Wilds is known for being a poorly optimized mess at times on PC. That holds true on here. It does a great job, that game gives the RTX 5080 in my main gaming desktop some trouble every now and then. So the fact this plays that game so well with the exception of some micro stuttering here and there, is great. 


The Acer Predator Neo Gaming Laptop is a a fantastic machine for doing battle in another world or doing the mundane normal every day tasks like, watching a video, homework or surfing the interwebs!  Highly recommended for those that live and work in the real world but like to take time out to fight in a Galaxy not so Far, Far Away.

reviews.title: Sharp 2.5K Display, Powerful, and Lightweight
reviews.content:
Acer now has in the Predator Neo line of gaming laptops, the Predator Neo 16S AI.  With it’s 16” 2.5k OLED display, a Core Ultra 9 Series 2 processor, and an RTX 5070 Ti, it makes for a really good upper entry level gaming laptop.


CPU/RAM
The Predator Neo comes with an Intel Core Ultra 9 Series 2 CPU.  This is a good CPU which certainly helps with Games and makes the Neo’s responsiveness fast and snappy.  It also comes with 16GB of DDR5 RAM.  This is still a base amount of RAM for an entry level gaming laptop, but I feel that it should have been stepped up to 32GB.  Given the RAM situation in 2026, keeping the base 16GB of RAM is a way to cut costs.  Though, I can upgrade later if I want to.  This does have an impact of RAM intensive games.  Battlefield 6 sessions were maxing out the RAM on the Neo.  The game still played well, but 32GB would have helped.


GPU/Display
The 16” 2.5K OLED display is the best laptop screen I’ve seen.  It’s crisp, vibrant, and has an incredibly high refresh rate.  It makes for a very pleasant FPS gaming experience.  When playing Battlefield 6, I was getting up to 80 FPS at 2.5K resolution with the Turbo profile on.  The limitation involved three things.  The GPU, VRAM, and system RAM.  The CPU wasn’t maxed out, but the RTX 5070 Ti laptop GPU with 12GB of VRAM and the 16GB of system RAM were maxed out.  If the laptop had 32GB of RAM and the GPU had 16GB of VRAM, I would have gotten higher frame rates, but this is, due to the GPU, VRAM, and system RAM, an entry level laptop, albeit the upper end of entry level.


Other Components
It has Killer WiFi and wired NICs.  I was getting up to 850Mbps for downloads over my wireless connection with multiple walls between the Neo and my router.  The 1TB NVMe SSD is a step up from previous generation laptops at this level.  There is plenty of space to hold multiple FPS, RTS, and RPGs that I have along with many LLMs.  The keyboard has RGB lighting and the keys feel good.  It has a full keyboard including num pad.  The trackpad is large and smooth.  Acer added in an RGB lighted button for quick switching through the different power profiles.  I can quickly go from Quiet to Balanced to Power to Turbo and I can see what profile the Neo is currently using by the color of the RGB light of the button.  I’m glad Acer added that in. 


Ports
There are a good number of ports on the Neo.  It has a USB-A 3.2 Gen 1 port, a micro-SD card reader, RJ-45 ethernet port, and a microphone/headphone jack on the left side.  On the right is a USB-A 3.2 port, a USB-A 3.2 that allows for charging a device even when the laptop is off.  On the Back is a full HDMI 2.1 port, Thunderbolt 4 type C port, USB-C DC-in port (supports PD fast charging up to 100W), and the power adapter DC-in port.  


Software
Acer includes the Predator Sense application.  This is where I can set different power profiles, run checks on the RAM, Battery, and SSD, monitor CPU and GPU information.  Acer also has a few additional programs that can be installed on the Neo that involve AI.  One is an chat interface to LLMs.  It gives me the option to use either of two Llama models or Gemini.  It’s convenient as I don’t have to open a browser to use Gemini or download something like Ollama to use either of the two Llama models locally.  I would like to see support for more local models, but I’m happy to see Acer include this.  I hope they update the app later to support other LLMs.


Final Thoughts
I suspect the 16GB of DDR5 and the 12GB of VRAM was a cost savings decision by Acer given the global RAM and VRAM situation we have in 2026.  Even with that, the performance is really good for an entry level laptop and the high refresh rate of the 2.5K OLED display make for a good gaming experience.  Thumbs up to Acer regarding the display.  The laptop is light compared to other gaming laptops which I’m thankful for.  Carrying this in my laptop backpack will be less burdensome given how light it is and the power block being of a reasonable size and weight.

Overall, I’m happy with the direction Acer is going with the Predator Neo.  If you are looking for an upper end entry level laptop with an incredible display, then definitely consider the Acer Predator Neo 16S AI gaming laptop.

reviews.title: Pricey Mid-Range Acer Gaming Laptop
reviews.content:
After receiving this Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI gaming laptop, setting it up, and then testing it out on the games I enjoy playing, I found myself to be “low key” underwhelmed, which ultimately affected whether or not I could recommend this laptop.

First off, the laptop’s plastic chassis feels rather cheap, and not what I’d expect from a nearly $3000 retail price gaming laptop. The laptop being thin and lightweight doesn’t bother me, just as long as the fans do their job, vents are placed adequately, and the overall design reflects the requirements for managing the heat generated by modern gaming laptops.

I’m well aware that computer components are at a premium at the time of this review. So I was relieved to find that this Acer Predator has a 1TB SSD, rather than the 512gb many gaming laptops seem to come equipped with, by default. These days, having a minimum of 1TB storage on a gaming laptop/PC, is a necessity, imo. The NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Ti graphics card is oh so sweet! The Intel Core Ultra 9 series (2026) processor has more than proven itself so far, even though I generally prefer AMD Ryzen processors. I would have liked to have double the RAM, but 16gb is still able to handle the types of games I usually play. Plus, there’s always the option to install more RAM as need, and your budget, allows.

Onboard speakers are average; sound could definitely be better. As many gamers do, perhaps consider a soundbar or computer speakers, although a gaming headset is also a viable way to go. The webcam is pretty standard, but I did notice some fuzziness and pixelization no matter the light in the room, or what settings I tweaked to try and improve the picture quality.

However, the 16” OLED screen is absolutely beautiful! The colors simply pop; the visuals are crisp and clear. Black pixels were indeed truer. Screen brightness and clarity remained consistent even looking at the screen from the side rather than straight on. I could absolutely tell that difference between this OLED screen and the LED one on my other gaming laptop.

Additional notable features:

Slim profile; simple, stylish design.
Matte finish won’t show fingerprints.
Acer did a great job of including an ideal number and types of ports.
Fans were relatively quiet, and while I didn’t find the laptop to run particularly ‘hot’, still do allow for plenty of airflow.
Exhaust vents on back of hinge and along both sides.
Large hinge is not at all flimsy.
Four elongated rubberized feet for stability.
Acer included a nice zippered slipcover carrying case, which is very cool.

I was pleased to not have to remove a ton of bloatware. Just needed to delete the offered McAfee virus protection ‘free trial’. To me, I’d rather use Windows Defender anyway, and decide later if I want to purchase additional security of my choice. Part of the setup process is deciding what software you need/want, and what to keep that may be pre-installed on your machine. I found Predator Sense to be a useful tool for monitoring the laptop’s stats, etc.

*Remember to do available Windows updates, and any necessary updates to drivers, BIOS, and preferred software, etc. during your initial setup and customization process.

Gameplay on this laptop was fun. Playing my usual games - Warcraft, Guild Wars 2, Baldur’s Gate 3, and various Steam client games - was a delight. For most games, I could keep many of my in-game graphical settings at mid-level; with a few select game customizations on high. I still had to choose what mattered most, along with fine tuning some settings as this laptop is by no means “high-end.” Both the NVIDIA RTX 5070 Ti and OLED screen helped contribute to my overall gaming experience.

Bottom line - While the actual components in this gaming laptop are pretty solid, and perform as intended, even being a “mid-range” choice, I know there are other comparable options out there, and I would suggest exploring those before choosing this Acer. That said, I would only recommend this model laptop with some reservations, based on what I’ve stated in this review.

reviews.title: A Good Laptop With Some Tough Compromises
reviews.content:
📦 UNBOXING:

Inside the box, you’ll find the laptop, a 230W charging brick, and a fabric laptop sleeve with zipper. Also inside the box is some basic documentation. Everything was packaged well, and used a lot of recyclable material.

💪 BUILD:

The Predator Helios Neo 16S AI seems to use a mix of metal and plastic for its chassis design. While it won’t feel as premium as some more expensive slim profile gaming laptops, it doesn’t feel cheap, either. Notably, this laptop also has a rear thermal shelf making its footprint a bit larger than traditional 16” laptops.

Unfortunately, my unit has some bulge at the center of the display hinge, so it protrudes a bit when the lid is shut. This may be from overtightening the hinge from the factory, but I’d expect better at this price point.

At 4.86 lbs on my food-grade scale, there are lighter gaming laptops on the market, but it’s certainly not anywhere near close to the “desktop replacement” laptops that have much thicker designs. It still remains quite thin at a maximum thickness of 0.74 inches on its tapered design.

🔌PORTS:

The Helios Neo 16S AI is well-equipped with ports that most users would care about.

On the left, you have a 2.5G slim ethernet port, a USB 3.2 gen 1 Type-A port, a MicroSD card reader that maxes out at UHS-I speeds, and a 3.5mm audio combo jack. On the right, you have 2x USB 3.2 gen 2 Type-A ports and status LED indicators.

And on the rear, you have a DC barrel input for 230W power, an HDMI 2.1 port, a Thunderbolt 4 Type-C port, and a USB 3.2 gen 2 Type-C port (with DisplayPort). Both Type-C ports support charging at 90 W / 100 W at 20 V. Lower wattage USB-C PD chargers may not work well with this laptop, so plan accordingly.

Overall, I’m happy with the port selection Acer is offering on this laptop. Connecting a mouse, headset, and keyboard to this laptop simultaneously is easy, and those with Thunderbolt docking stations can further simplify their desk setups.

🔧 EXPANSION & UPGRADES:

Unscrewing the (10) T6 torx screws on the bottom panel, you’ll find a few upgrade points for this laptop. There are 2x m.2 2880 PCIe 4.0 NVMe slots on this laptop, with one occupied by a 1TB Kingston OM8PJP41024K3-CA0 in my unit.

Additionally, there are 2x SODIMM slots pre-populated with 2x 8GB SK Hynix HMCG66AHBVA315N CSODIMMs in my unit, but it should support 2x 32GB CSODIMMs of DDR5 memory at 6400MT/s. Given the cost of memory these days, I cannot overstate how great it is that you can upgrade to a higher capacity later if/when it becomes more affordable.

Lastly, there is a Killer Wi-Fi 6E AX1675i adapter installed in a m.2 2230 slot. So if down the line you need to upgrade the Wi-Fi card, it should be quite easy to do.

⌨️ ​KEYBOARD & TOUCHPAD:

The Neo 16S AI has a good keyboard. I’m generally able to achieve ~100 wpm with high accuracy. It’s easy to type on without being loud or annoying. It also supports 4 zones of RGB by dividing up the keyboard into 4 equal sections. This allows for some different RGB effects, but you can also keep it simple with a static color, as well.

The mechanical touchpad uses the Microsoft Precision driver, so it supports multi-touch gestures without issue. However, the touchpad is on the smaller side compared to some other laptops. With that said, I didn’t find it to be so small that it was a hindrance to use. It also uses matte plastic instead of etched glass, so it may wear down from fingerprint oils over time. Physical clicks will be best done towards the bottom of the touchpad, as the top has much more resistance to click.

📺 DISPLAY:

Onboard the laptop is the Samsung SDC41AB—a 16” 240Hz OLED panel that supports G-SYNC and is DisplayHDR True Black 500 certified. What this means is excellent response times, superb motion clarity, deep contrast, rich colors, and gets plenty bright. It is a glossy panel, so it does have reflective properties. If you plan to do a lot of gaming on this display, you’ll find it to be a joy. One thing that I noticed out of the box is that despite being a 10-bit panel, 8-bit color is enabled by default, so I’d recommend opening the Intel Graphics Software app and changing the Color Depth setting to enable 10-bit color. At minimum, that should help eliminate color banding across gradients.

The one notable downside is that this display is locked to 240Hz, which means it does not drop lower to save power. Many laptops of this caliber would still have the ability to drop to 60Hz, but Acer opted not to do so, and I think that’s a real miss.

But after researching more about this locked framerate, I was able to use Custom Resolution Utility (CRU) to add a 120Hz mode, but the display gets much dimmer in this mode, and it loses color accuracy. It’s not an ideal solution, but it can be a useful workaround if you want to save power while on battery—more on that later.

📹​ WEBCAM & MICROPHONE:

The 1080p IR webcam supports Windows Hello facial recognition, and delivers a reasonably sharp image quality in good lighting conditions. It does not fare so well in darker lighting conditions, which remains a common issue on the vast majority of laptop webcams.

Two integrated microphones flank the webcam, but there is also another one on the outer edge of the laptop to the right of the touchpad that is used for AI noise reduction. You can change the noise reduction settings via the Realtek Audio Console, or you can turn it off and use Microsoft’s Voice Clarity feature in the Windows microphone settings. Either way, the integrated microphone should be plenty decent for calls.

🔊 SPEAKERS & HEADPHONE:

One of the cost-saving measures for this laptop design was the speakers. Frankly, they’re not great. They are bottom-firing which makes them sound tinnier, and with only 2 small drivers, there isn’t really any bass. So you’re really going to be best off using headphones, as these speakers don’t deliver a very immersive experience. Even with the DTS:X Ultra app, trying to customize a sound profile for these laptop speakers won’t yield something that I’m going to enjoy, but they can be made somewhat passable with a bit of EQ.

The 3.5mm headphone output is also reasonably good for higher sensitivity headphones and can drive a pair like the Sennheiser HD 560S without issue. I also tried a low sensitivity headphone like the Dan Clark Expanse, and the headphone was able to deliver comfortably loud volumes, and even exceed what I would want. By default, DTS:X Ultra is enabled for headphones, too, but it can be disabled for headphone output. If you want the purest listening experience, I recommend disabling DTS:X Ultra for headphones and also disabling audio enhancements and spatial sound in the windows sound settings for the headphone output.

⚡ PERFORMANCE:

This model uses an Intel Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus with 8 P-Cores and 16 E-Cores. It’s an iterative improvement on Core Ultra 9 285HX that yields about an 8% average improvement in performance for gaming. While it won’t take the crown of best mobile CPUs for gaming, it certainly stands high up on the charts.

More importantly, the mobile NVIDIA RTX 5070 Ti has 12GB of GDDR7 RAM with a maximum graphics power of 115W, so you should expect less performance than a bulkier laptop with a 140W maximum graphics power. If you want to maximize performance, use a laptop stand and use the turbo profile and additionally set the fan control to max. While the fans are loud in this configuration, it does well to dissipate heat and keep the system from thermal throttling.

I was able to achieve a 3DMark Time Spy score of 16227. High-end games like Cyberpunk 2077 can even run with path tracing at over 60fps using DLSS and frame generation. In my testing, the GPU mostly sustained around 100W of power with some occasional bursts to 115W.

I feel it’s quite unfortunate that this system comes with only 16GB of RAM @ 6400 MT/s, and some of this is reserved for Intel integrated graphics, as well. Even after a bit of debloating, Windows still consumes a lot of memory. If multitasking with a web browser, discord, and a high-end game, it’s a lot more likely that Windows will need to pagefile to the SSD which can lead to stutters and make the system feel less responsive.

I was able to find a used kit of 2x16GB SODIMMs @ 5600MT/s in my local market for $200 (a good deal in this market), and this improved my ability to have more applications running. In 3DMark Time Spy, this RAM yielded a < 2% difference in performance degradation from the stock 6400MT/s kit.

Overall, performance is good for a slim-class gaming laptop and is even competitive with more premium slim designs.

🔋 BATTERY:

Battery is one of the bigger shortcomings of this laptop. Despite the 92Whr battery, power consumption remains high due to the high refresh rate display, applications running on the Nvidia Graphics, and the CPU turboing while on battery.

Changing the maximum processor state on battery to 99% down from 100% can prevent the CPU from turboing. Using a custom 120Hz refresh rate and lower brightness can reduce power consumption fairly significantly. Using the Eco mode while on battery can prolong its use, and ensuring apps aren’t using the Nvidia Graphics while on battery can further stretch the battery life.

With all of these changes, you’re likely to see only 2-4 hours of battery with light usage.

🧐 CONCLUSION:

I have mixed feelings about the Helios Neo 16S AI. Plugged in, performance is actually reasonably good for a slim gaming laptop. But unplugged, battery life is quite poor compared to its competition. It has a great display that unfortunately lacks a 60hz mode for battery saving, has a good array of ports and is pretty quiet while on battery. Upgradable RAM and the ability to add another SSD is great, but its build quality is mid-tier. The previous model with a Core Ultra 9 275HX and 32GB of RAM costs significantly less while delivering similar performance. My recommendation? Wait for a sale.

reviews.title: Power & Pixels All In A Slim Package You'll Love!!
reviews.content:
I picked up the new Acer Predator Neo with the OLED screen and the RTX 5070 Ti, and overall it’s a really solid machine packed with some great features, though it still has a few quirks you should know about.

**The Good:**

* **That screen is drop-dead gorgeous:** The picture quality is amazing. Because it’s an OLED screen, the colors pop, the blacks are pitch black, and games look stunning. Plus, the high refresh rate makes everything look super smooth.
* **Ports are in all the right places:** I really love that many of the main cables (like the power and video plugs) go into the *back* of the laptop instead of the sides. This keeps all the wires away from your mouse hand, which makes your desk look and feel way cleaner.
* **Incredible performance for the price:** For what you pay compared to other high-end brands, you get a ton of gaming power. It handles heavy games and multitasking smoothly without stuttering during normal play.
* **Fast loading and plenty of room:** With a fast processor and 1TB of storage, everything boots up in seconds, and you have plenty of space to install a bunch of large games without constantly deleting things.

**The Bad:**

* **It runs hot and gets loud:** Because I believe they made the laptop thinner in there, the fans have to work extra hard. When you push it with heavy gaming, it gets pretty hot and loud, and the internal parts have to slow down a bit to keep from overheating.
* **The sound isn't great:** The built-in speakers sound tinny and lack bass, so you'll definitely want to use a good pair of headphones.
* **It feels a bit light for my taste:** Even though it’s thinner, I personally prefer a thicker, heavier feel because it makes a laptop feel sturdier and higher quality. This one feels a bit too lightweight and plastic-y in places.

**The Bottom Line:**
If you want an incredible screen, great ports layout, and awesome performance without spending a fortune, this is a fantastic computer. However, if you care more about heavy-duty metal build quality and a thick, tank-like feel, you might want to look at a bulkier model.
