q_a.question: Are there an geographic restrictions to where this Windows 11 LIcense can be activated and used. I'm interested in buy this laptop as a gift for someone who resides in another country?
q_a.answer: The Windows license built into a computer travels with it and is valid anywhere in the world. It is permanently injected into the motherboard's physical hardware chips by the factory, it is not region-locked, and Microsoft will automatically activate it over the internet whether you boot it up in Europe, Asia, Africa, or the Americas. If purchased in another country, however, you may not be able to change the language if you travel outside that country without an additional cost. Also, if you are concerned about MS365 (formerly Office), that IS Region-Locked. it will often fail to activate if your Microsoft Account's location or IP address points to a different continent. Finally, while Lenovo includes an International Warranty Service (IWS) on many machines, it has severe limitations: Lenovo will only repair your laptop in another country if that exact model variant is also officially sold and supported by Lenovo in that destination country, and because your IdeaPad is a US-market consumer model, a Lenovo repair facility in another country may refuse to service it simply because they do not stock the US-spec replacement motherboards or keyboards.

q_a.question: Can you stop calling Full High Definition as the acronym 2K? It is very misleading, as that is not a standard resolution name and can be mistaken for QHD aka 2560x1440
q_a.answer:
Hey mpetersen71,

We appreciate your inquiry and concern that you've shared. To address this, we'd like to share some reasoning as to why 2K has taken off and is now used widely across the computing space. 

2K resolution is one of multiple high-definition image resolution standards. The primary difference is that 2K resolution can refer to more than one image size. For this reason, 2K is generally accepted as an umbrella term. It is typically used when referring to the motion picture industry, as many films are projected at this standard.

These resolutions are defined by the Digital Cinema Initiatives, or DCI, a governing body comprised of major motion picture studios. The 1920x1200 resolution is considered as 2K, as the horizontal resolution (number of pixels across the display) meets the parameters to fall under the 2K umbrella. 

If you'd like to learn even more, you can visit the following Lenovo web address for details: 
https://www.lenovo.com/us/en/faqs/pc-life-faqs/what-is-2k-resolution/?orgRef=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.google.com%252F | 

We hope that this helps, and if you have any other questions, please feel free to reach out!

reviews.title: Outstanding value and quality
reviews.content:
I waited a bit to write the review to see how it would perform over time. I've had it for about 6 months now and it's been fantastic - no issues whatsoever. It's being used with a MacBook Pro for a home office and normal office tasks - not media work.

The VESA mount works well, no installation issues. I am not using the provided stand so cannot speak to that. But mounts are not a big investment and improve the ergonomics of any monitor.

Screen quality is great, especially if you work with a lot of white background documents. White is uniform across screen, no moire patterns, no dim areas, no white hue transitions etc. Looks beautiful. I purchased a more expensive LG monitor which had noticeable patterns and I ended up returning that one and picked up this one. Saved money and got a better product. I was on the fence about returning that one because I thought maybe all screens have minor issues - nope, this one looks crystal clear.

The built in speakers are a nice addition. I sometimes listen to Pandora or NPR or podcasts in the background and they are perfectly nice - pls don't expect Bose performance form a monitor speaker.

Can't speak to the negative experiences of the other buyers here but I have not had any of the issues mentioned. I have no negatives to mention. I actually like everything about this monitor.

reviews.title: Great laptop, fast, and excellent battery life
reviews.content:
I wanted a laptop for traveling and tried out a few others before deciding on this one. The build quality is great, it definitely feels like a premium laptop with the ceraluminum finish, the hinges feel very sturdy and don't wobble back and forth like some other laptops. Since the weight is only about 2.8lbs, it's a big plus for travel. 

The screen, like others have mentioned with these laptops, does have some glare/reflection to it, but it doesn't bother me. The screen can get very bright, which is a good thing, but I can comfortably keep it at 20-30% brightness at home and not have any issues with viewing.

Once I was able to get it setup, download all the necessary drivers, and fine-tune the text/window scaling that Windows loves to over-scale, the usability greatly increased.
The battery life is excellent. I'm used to a 15.6" Lenovo Legion Slim 7 with an RTX 3060 and max 4-5 hour of battery life (being generous of course), so when I saw 12 or 13 hours of battery remaining after a few hours of use, I was pleasantly surprised.  

Although the processor doesn't have the upgraded iGPU like the 386H and 388H, I'm still able to run Solidworks without any issues after some minor performance tweaks and allow-listing the Intel Graphics (the RAM fills up very quickly if you don't), now I barely surpass 16gb usage without any other major programs running. I can have almost a dozen Brave tabs open, Cursor IDE running, and a few other processes and still don't notice any slowdown.

The 1TB SSD was a big selling point for me rather than the 512gb being used in what seems like every laptop now. I dual-boot Linux Fedora and like to use it as a daily driver, so being able to partition off a good chunk for that, and still have plenty of room for Windows programs is very nice.

Overall, if you have the budget and don't need the upgraded iGPU like me, I would recommend at least testing this laptop out.

reviews.title: MOTHERBOARD FIRMWARE ENGINEERING DEFECT NOT FIXABL
reviews.content: I purchased the Lenovo Yoga 7i and encountered a deep firmware‑level engineering defect that cannot be fixed, even after Lenovo replaced both the motherboard and SSD. The laptop intermittently loses NVMe identity and falls back to a SCSI controller data link, which severely impacts only random reads/writes while leaving sequential performance untouched. Because of that, casual users—and even gamers—would never notice the problem, but it becomes obvious to anyone who monitors system responsiveness or low‑level storage behavior. Windows remained in perfect health throughout, proving the issue is rooted in the Yoga 7i’s fragile firmware design rather than any replaceable component. I was a few days past the 60‑day Total Care return window, but the Best Buy general manager listened, understood the engineering defect, and graciously approved a full refund. I appreciate Best Buy for standing behind their customers and handling a difficult firmware issue with professionalism.

reviews.title: Great Laptop with minor caveats
reviews.content:
With the current electronic market I do feel like it's very hard to find a perfect laptop under $2k but this is a very good option. I use this for personal web browsing and art with light gaming.

Let me start with the cons of this laptop. The main issues I have with the laptop are due to the configurations available at Bestbuy. 
1. There is no option for 1tb of storage for this model. 512gb is simply not enough storage for most people long term. Add on the fact that Lenovo + the Windows AI crap has a bunch of nonsense apps loaded on by default and after the initial system updates, you start off with about 80gb of your storage used up as soon as you boot it up. There is not an additional slot on the mobo to upgrade this btw you will have to get an external drive down the line.
2. There is no option for the 120hz model(for some reason, this option is just not available in the US??) I feel like in 2026 a 60hz screen on a system over $1k is a bit ridiculous. Odds are your phone has 120hz (my ipad from 2020 even has 120hz screen). Considering the amount of power in the CPU it also feels like a waste. Another issue is during the day the screen simply does not get bright enough. The screen is also super glossy so the glare you get is insane if you use it in a bright environment. 
3. The pen is not included and also not sold at bestbuy. I can understand for most people this is a non issue but I feel like by not even having the option I am missing out on an entire feature of the laptop. (I ended up getting one separately and it’s good for light art and notetaking [not practical for notetaking because of the laptop size] but while the pen is great there’s some weird windows software issues that pop up and cause lagging issues)
This is a nitpick but the charging cord is a bit short for me personally and unfortunately the cord is embedded into the block so if I wanted a longer cord I would have to get a 65watt block and cord. Also coming from a gaming laptop to me the laptop is light but to others it might be heavy.

Onto the Pros, this laptop is FAST, with 24GB of RAM and the intel i7 chip you can multitask and do work without being slowed down by your system. If you’re like me and tend to have a lot of things open at once this is fantastic. The laptop can also handle some light gaming, I played some Fields of Mistria, Stardew, and Spirit City and they all ran fine after adjusting some settings. I will say the 60hz screen definitely was noticeable to me while gaming(it makes things feel like there’s motion blur on). If you’re prone to motion sickness I’d be aware of that; you can change some settings to help but at the end of the day it will still be a 60hz screen. The color accuracy on this laptop is great, a bit oversaturated but good enough for me to continue doing my art. The keyboard is the best I’ve ever used on a laptop; I really like it(but it is a bit of a fingerprint magnet with hand oils). The fans are very quiet and the laptop barely even gets warm for me even when I gamed. The battery life for me has been great and lasts me all day but I don’t travel as much as others so I haven’t used it on battery alone for anything outside of web browsing.

reviews.title: G16 3k gaming laptop
reviews.content:
I’ve been very impressed with the G16 gaming laptop. The performance is excellent—it handles gaming, multitasking, and everyday use without any problems. Games run smooth, the display looks sharp and vibrant, and the high refresh rate makes everything feel fast and responsive.

reviews.title: Wonderful laptop

reviews.title: High Performing Platform - Great Gaming Laptop
reviews.content:
The 2026 Asus ROG Zephyrus G16 is a light refresh to the 2025 model, which brings a few changes to the chassis and updates to the processor, which deliver some decent performance and efficiency gains. Without any new releases from NVidia, the GPU is still a 5XXX series from NVidia. The G16 is still a very capable gaming powerhouse in an Ultrabook’s body. I have a 2025 model with a 5070, so I am able to make some pretty direct comparisons.

Specs 

Processor – Intel Core Ultra 9 386H - CPU 16C/16T @ 2.1 GHz with boost to 4.9 GHz 
Graphics – NVidia GeForce RTX 5080 Laptop GPU w/ 16GB GDDR7 @ 1500 MHz
                    Intel Xe3 4 core onboard the Processor w/ max boost to 2.5 GHz
Memory – Onboard 32B LPDDR5X 8533 Dual Channel (92-80-80-180)
Storage – 1TB PCI-e Gen4x4 NVME SK Hynix HFS001TEJ9X101N 
Display - 16” 2560 x 1600p 16:10 (WQXGA) OLED screen @240HZ, 0.2ms, 100% DCI-P3, G-Sync
Camera – 1080p IR Webcam with Windows Hello
Network Adapter – 802.11be (WiFi 7 Triple Band) adapter / Bluetooth 6.0 Radio 
Ports – 1X USB 4 Type-C with DisplayPort and power delivery / 1X USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C with DisplayPort / 2X USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A / 1X HDMI 2.1 / 3.5mm TRRS jacks for headsets / 1 SD Reader
Battery – 90Wh – 30min for 0-50% charging and 8-10 hours of web browsing and some light gaming
OS – Windows 11 Home – a few preinstalled ASUS utilities 

Design 

This generation of the G16 doesn’t deviate much from the 2025 model in terms of design. The layout and aesthetic are almost identical with some upgrades. The body remains a machined aluminum 6063 chassis that is thin and sturdy – it retains a very premium feel. The design is sleek and while it has gaming looks it doesn’t scream it. The slash lighting and RGB keyboard are the only real hints to the gaming keyboard chops. The fit/finish of the aluminum chassis, the thin profile, and the Eclipse Gray finish makes the G16 appear to be a professional looking device. As with other ASUS devices this comes bundled with their Armoury Crate software suite. The software is what allows you to customize the lighting on the LED slash, and the RGB keyboard.

The hinge has been upgraded for this year (Easy Lift Hinge 2.0), but still keeps its 135° opening range. The hinge handles the torque of opening the lid better than last years, which is true. Its’s a nice quality of life upgrade. Dimensionally the 2026 model is identical to last years with a 4.3lb weight, and a slim 0.69” thickness. The laptop is 13.94” wide, and that is entirely utilized by the 16” screen. 

This years G16 sticks with the Intel based system and utilizes the new Ultra 9 386H. The 386H at first seemed like a step down from last years 285H, which has a slightly higher base clock and boost clock. However, the 386H brings decent thermal/power efficiency gains while maintaining a similar performance level. My benchmarks put the 386H slightly ahead in some tasks, but where clockspeed decided things, the 386H fell about 3-5% behind. The 386H has a similar architecture with 16 cores and 16 threads of processing. These 16 cores are broken up into 3 groups – performance, efficiency, and low power efficiency. The efficiency and low power cores are where the 386H made its biggest improvements, which extends battery life and reduces the thermal load on the system. The onboard graphics card is a Nvidia 5080 16GB mobile GPU. The 5080 supports DX12 Ultimate, ray tracing and DLSS 4.0. The laptop can be connected to multiple external monitors through the HDMI 2.1 port or through Type-C ports (they all support DisplayPort). Your monitor count is limited by the bandwidth each monitor needs. 

The G16 comes with a 32GB of LPDDR5X 8533 RAM in dual channel mode. The RAM is integrated into the motherboard, and there are no additional slots for expansion. With the current RAM market, this is a big contributor to the cost of this machine. It’s unfortunate that the RAM is not user upgradeable, otherwise you could get a lower spec’d system to upgrade later. With 32GB there’s not much this system can’t handle, so if you think you will need the extra memory bandwidth then 32GB is the way to go. I do CAD/3D modeling, so the extra RAM is appreciated over my 2025 G16, which only has 16GB. For gaming 32GB is only a benefit to some games, and is in no way a requirement for most games. Storage comes in the form of a 1TB PCIe 4.0 M.2 2280 NVME drive from SK Hynix. There is one additional slot available so your storage can easily be expanded beyond the initial 1TB. 

The display is a 16” 2560 x 1600p OLED screen with a 240Hz refresh rate and a 0.2ms response time, and 1100 nits of brightness. ASUS calls this their Nebula Display. At this resolution you come away with a 188.7 PPI density. The 0.2 ms response time is right in line with what OLED’s can provide. At 1100 nits of peak brightness this years display is more than twice as bright as 2025’s, and it easily clears the brightness requirements for HDR content. The display carries Pantone color validation along with a 100% DCI-P3 color gamut, and a Delta E <1. The laptop seamlessly switches between the 5080 and the Intel Xe3 graphics with its MUX switch and Nvidia Advanced Optimus. Depending on the graphical processing load the system will toggle automatically between the onboard and discrete GPU. The screen itself is excellent to view any content on. The OLED has very good color representation and the peak brightness provides an even greater contrast to the deep blacks that an OLED can produce. Off-angle viewing is great as well and I had no problem seeing the screen in any lighting condition.

Games and Benchmarking 

I ran the G16 through the same series of benchmarks (3DMark Time Spy and Steel Nomad, GeekBench 7, PCMark, Cinebench R23, Dirt Rally Benchmark, and Shadow of War Benchmark) that I use to test my all of my PC’s. I included a screenshot of my raw results. The gaming benchmarks show that this is a high performing system at 3K, 1440p, and 1080p. I saw real gains over my 2025 system with a 5070 and 16GB of RAM. I showed the ∆ for the relevant benchmarks. CPU related benchmarks showed a slight decrease in performance (3-5%), but areas where the additional RAM was a benefit the difference was quite large. The same goes for the GPU heavy benchmarks where the additional horsepower of the 5080 and its 16GB of VRAM (5070 has 8GB) gave it a decent edge. Benchmarks that were more CPU bound, i.e. 1080p gaming saw limited gains or even decreased performance. However, in all cases the framerates were still very high (~150fps+).

One of the benefits to the refresh is the improved cooling characteristics. The CPU being more thermally efficient and the vapor chamber design for the GPU helped decrease the heat output under load. The 2025 G16 would feel pretty warm under heavy/max loads, and in some cases it was uncomfortable to rest on my lap if the bottom touched bare skin. This years G16 has made some improvements in that area, and I can feel the temp drop. The bottom of the chassis gets warm under normal usage, but definitely less than the previous gen which I appreciate. Under heavy usage the chassis still gets very warm though. The system fans under full load do a good job keeping the temps in check and they aren’t overly loud.

I played several games to test the real life performance . The main game I played was Halo Infinite through Gamepass. The laptop comes with a 2-month Gamepass code. Ultra settings @3K looked great. The in-game resource monitor showed ultra settings would need just under 8GB of VRAM, so with 16GB of VRAM I had plenty of overhead. I played several matches and saw my framerate hover around 140fps, with dips down to 115 at the bottom. This is a decent step up over the 5070 based system which played around 120FPS on high settings. That extra bit of VRAM really goes a long ways towards bumping up the performance. Turning the resolution to 1080p my frames jumped to 175 with lows around 140. There really isn’t even a need to play on lower settings with this CPU/GPU combo. 

Keyboard and Trackpad

The keyboard is a tenkeyless full RGB chiclet membrane design. The RGB lighting is not per-key addressable. The keyboard is identical to the 2025 model, which I have enjoyed typing on. It’s a quiet typing keyboard that has a good feel to the keys – better than most laptop keyboards I have typed on. The key travel is 1.7mm which means you actually have some depth to the keys. With the lighting on the keys really shine and pass the light through easily. With the lighting off you will be hard pressed to see the keys in anything other than a decently lit room.

The trackpad is good as well. It sits right around 6 x 4”, and it takes up the entire distance from the front of the laptop to the spacebar. It has good gesture registration and the click feels good as well. I’m not a big trackpad user, but this is a good one that is easy to live with. 

Final Thoughts 

The 2026 G16 brings some modest system updates from the 2025 model – they really didn’t mess with the formula too much. The 32GB of RAM and 16GB 5080 provide the system resources and horsepower to make this configuration shine. The screen is beautiful and bright. It will handle any AAA game you toss at it without much issue, and do so at high/ultra settings. Its got a great lightweight design, which makes it easy to toss into the laptop bag and not feel like I’m carrying around a lead weight. The only downside to this platform, and the same was true of the 2025 model, is the use of onboard RAM modules. I can’t imagine I will need more system memory than the 32GB this one has, but in the current RAM and SSD pricing landscape, it would be nice to have the option of a lower spec’d system that you can upgrade later when the pricing returns to “normal” again. This is a great platform – I have really liked the G14/G16 lineup over the years, and have recommended it to many people. This model is no different. ASUS did a great job again.

reviews.title: Amazing Computer!
reviews.content: I have had numerous versions of the Zephyrus over the course of time, primarily the G14 models. This is by far the best instance I have had. Tremendous build quality, the OLED is worth the hype and I am amazed that the 5080 can be cooled in such a thin laptop.

reviews.title: Excellent gaming Laptop
reviews.content: Coming from the Asus Zephyrus G16 with an RTX 4080, I expected an upgrade — but calling this “better” is honestly an understatement. The 5080 paired with the new Panther Lake CPU feels like a true generational leap. Games run noticeably smoother, 1% lows are higher, and multitasking across split monitors is effortless.One of the biggest improvements is how future‑proof this hardware feels. The 4080’s 12GB VRAM was a real limitation for ray tracing, but that bottleneck is gone here. Whether it’s productivity or play, the system handles everything: office work with multiple screens and programs, or even 4K gaming while streaming at the same time. It just does it all.

reviews.title: Great improvements for 2026
reviews.content:
ASUS has done it again with this flagship gaming laptop. I own several of the previous G16 models and I will say they are better than my gaming desktop. They are sleek and come with everything you need to be able to game on the go. I have traveled all over the world and always have my Asus ROG Zephyrus with me. Whether you are into gaming, creating, or just productivity this is one of the best laptops on the market. 

Design:

ASUS designed this laptop with a premium aluminum body that is both lightweight and thin. The body is made from a CNC-milled aluminum chassis carved from a single solid piece of metal, making it both stronger and lighter. ASUS included what they call ROG intelligent cooling system. A vapor chamber, heat pipe, and other cooling designs allow this laptop to run cooler and more efficient than ever. This not only gives you better performance, but it also means that it runs slightly quieter. The slash lighting on the front also offers expanded zones to give it smoother and more detailed lighting options. 

The display is one of the best I have seen in a package this size. It has a 3K resolution, a 240hz refresh rate and 1100 nits peak brightness. 

The keyboard and trackpad have good feedback and are more than enough for on the go. However, When I am at home I usually plug in to external peripherals or connect a controller depending on what type of game I am playing. 

Ports:

Due to the size of this laptop parts are somewhat limited but it has everything someone would need. It has 2 USB-A ports and 2 USB-C ports, one of each on either side. I love that ASUS did this because you have both USB types on either side. Especially when it comes to gaming, I have many older accessories that still use USB-A and then it also works with all the new USB-C accessories. It also has an HDMI, headphone jack, and SD card reader. It is nice that all these ports are included on a laptop that is thin. The SD card reader is a full-size card reader which is perfect for creators.   

Performance:

Performance is something that Zephyrus does well. It has some of the best components on the market and is a powerhouse. This CPU is a 16-core CPU and can handle anything you attempt to do with it. 10 of the 6 cores are efficiency cores and can-do everyday tasks. The extra 6 cores are performance cores which will kick in when you need all the power. It includes 32gbs of ram which is more than enough RAM for both creators and gamers. The SSD is 1TB which runs at extremely high transfer rates. The GeForce RTX 5080 is a top end graphics card that allows you to do or play anything you want. This laptop also includes 2 months free of Xbox game pass which allows you play hundreds of free games. This is a great service if you like to play many different types of games without having to buy all of them. 

Upgradability:

Unfortunately, like many other laptops on the market today, it has become harder to make your own upgrades. The good news is that this laptop has just about everything you need, and I do not see a need to upgrade any of the components. This is a tradeoff for having an extremely thing. Lightweight, efficient, and powerful machine. Quite frankly I am okay with this trade off. The only thing that might be worth doing is upgrading to a larger SSD if you play tons of games. If you are creator, I would recommend using external drives if you need extra space. 

Conclusion:

ASUS is one of the leaders in the gaming market. Especially when it comes to mobile gaming. Upgrades to the cooling system this year on the G16 make it even more powerful and competitive. If you are a gamer or creator and want the very best out there, then this is the laptop for you.

reviews.title: Build quality; battery life
reviews.content: This product's build quality was far superior to the 2025 model I tried beforehand, which had hinge creaking within weeks and a loose touchpad. It also worked perfectly from factory install, without requiring configuration to allow the computer's sleep mode to not reset the device. I use this around the house and occasionally outside as a EE/CPE student and light gamer.

reviews.title: Identity crisis causes performance loss
reviews.content:
This is a gaming laptop - that is thin and light. The combination of the two makes for what looks great on paper but really slices into the performance of what this machine really should be capable of had it been put into a larger chassis. Of course - then it would no longer be thin and light. It's a gaming machine that would look right at home in the board room (I've taken mine to work many times now - with the RGB and lid's lighting bar turned off nobody knew it was a gaming rig), but also is very capable of gaming when not in the office. The issue is this - the thin and light chassis doesn't allow for an adequate airflow for the max performance to be sustained - it starts off just fine but then thermal-throttles because it simply can't breathe enough.

The 3k screen is absolutely stunning - especially being that it's OLED, and at that resolution the 5080 GPU can crank out ample frame rates to make your games buttery smooth, BUT, why spend the extra on a 5080 when you can pretty much get the same performance from a NON thin and light laptop with a 5070? It's one of those odd compromises that really doesn't make a lot of sense to me.

I've compared this laptop to one that a friend has that has the same specs but is in one of the "traditional" thick and chonky laptop chassis - the same game was putting out AT MINIMUM 10% more frames per second than this one.

One other note - the RAM - it's soldered in directly to the board, so if you purchase one and decide you need more RAM, you're fairly stuck. Thankfully this model has 32GB, which is more than enough for *MOST* users unless you're a developer or running multiple virtual-machines. 

So, ultimately it's up to you - thin and light than can pass as a non-gaming PC but still game like a champ when it needs to , or spend less on a laptop with the same specs that looks the part and can stretch it's legs to reach it's full potential!

reviews.title: Incredibly high performance, super portable
reviews.content:
There's a lot to like about this laptop. First off, it looks great. The design rides a line between "obvious gaming laptop" and "professional workstation laptop", and you can configure the lighting however you want to lean one way or the other. The body is all metal, which both looks good and feels good to the touch. I like that the slash on the lid has configurable lines of lighting and can serve as a notification indicator if you have your laptop closed, or you can just turn it off and it looks like just a reflective accent. I don't have any complaints about the keyboard - it feels nice as far as laptop keyboards go - and I do appreciate the continued trend of ASUS putting dedicated volume and mic mute toggle keys away from the rest of the keyboard.

The performance is really good. The laptop 5080 still has the same amount of VRAM as the desktop variant, so you're not missing anything there; and it pairs really nicely with the Core Ultra 9. I've had really good performance when running anything from Stellar Blade on maximum settings to modded Minecraft, and local LLMs run pretty good as well if you like that sort of thing. The 32GB of RAM helps multitasking feel really comfortable, and I can reliably run a game with a Discord call open and keep a web page open in the background without having to close anything or make no background apps are running before I start the game. The screen also helps any games you play look *really* good - it's OLED, it has HDR support, it's 2560x1600 resolution, and you can pick from 60Hz or 240Hz refresh rate. I haven't run into any problems with the wireless card that would make it a problematic choice for online gaming, and while I would not advise allowing the bottom of this machine to actually sit on your lap while doing intense gaming (regular use is fine) the cooling system seems to be good enough to prevent noticeable thermal throttling (though I will say that I used this machine in environments that were already at a reasonable temperature and had good airflow - I do not know how well it would perform in a heat wave, for example). 

The overall user experience is also excellent. There are upward-facing speaker that help the laptop sound good when you're playing games or other kinds of media without headphones, and the webcam and microphone quality isn't awful. This laptop is "Copilot Plus," which I usually don't care *too* much about but features like the Windows Studio Effects for the camera or live captioning can be some quality-of-life upgrades. Apparently there's a Microsoft Pluton security processor in there, if you're worried about data security. As far as connecting your peripherals go, there's two USB ports, two USB-C ports, an HDMI port, an AUX port, and an SD card reader - honestly that's a really good selection. Of course, the biggest part of the user experience is how portable this machine is. It fits in a standard laptop bag, and while it's not the lightest thing in the world it's small and light enough to not be a pain to bring with you for on-the-go gaming or productivity or whatever. It really feels like this laptop hits way above its' size class in terms of performance.

As far as shortcomings go, there are two things I'm not super fond of. The battery life feels very underwhelming, even when on Battery Saver and not gaming. It's not quite so bad that I can watch it tick down before my eyes, but it does really ram home how much power all this hardware needs. I do wish it was a bit better when the discrete GPU was idling? I also think a fingerprint scanner for login would have been neat.

Overall, I'm a pretty big fan of this laptop. The market segment being targeted is very obviously the "high-end" segment, but when stacked up to that niche this machine absolutely delivers. If you're looking to get a top-of-the-line laptop that you anticipate taking with you a lot of places, or even if you're looking for a compact machine to replace a desktop computer, I can absolutely recommend this.

reviews.title: Incredible Power in Disguise
reviews.content:
The thing I love most about the Asus ROG Zephyrus G16 is the design. Build quality is phenomenal. The all-aluminum chassis feels premium no where you touch it. Despite its aluminum exterior and incredibly powerful internals, the chassis is 0.7” thick and only weighs 4.3 pounds. It's thin and light enough to fit into a standard 16" laptop sleeve and toss in a backpack. The only external features that might give away its gaming credentials are the slash lighting on the lid and the RGB keyboard. Both can be turned off, allowing you to go incognito and look like you’re using a pretty standard 16” laptop. 
On the inside, the combination of the Intel Core Ultra 9 386H, 32GB of RAM, and NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080 Laptop GPU cuts through pretty much everything like a hot knife through butter. Multitasking with tons of applications running and tabs galore in the background? No problem. Photo or video editing? No problem. The built-in SD card reader makes it convenient to pull files directly from your camera(s). Want to play virtually any AAA game? Again, no problem. I’m a Marvel Rivals addict and it runs like a dream, especially when combined with gig internet. Better hardware won’t automatically make you a better player, but it also can’t hurt, right?
The OLED display is stunning and feels huge. It's the kind of screen that makes everything look fantastic. The 240Hz refresh rate and G-SYNC make the laptop a FPS gamer’s dream.
Even the speakers surprised me. They produce surprisingly good sound for a laptop, with decent bass thanks to the two subwoofers, while higher-range vocals don't become tinny or washed out. I still prefer to use a headset, but using only the built in speakers and mic aren’t unpleasant if needed. 
I've used previous iterations of the Zephyrus G16, and one previous shortcoming was cooling. It's not exactly easy to keep this much performance cool inside such a thin chassis. I'm happy to report that Asus has made meaningful improvements here. The vapor chamber, advanced heatpipe design, liquid metal thermal compound, and redesigned high-efficiency exhaust system genuinely help keep temperatures under control while also making the laptop a bit quieter. Probably still a decent idea to use a cooling pad, but it’s no longer critical. 
Is the ROG Zephyrus G16 expensive? Oh yeah. Could you build a desktop with incredible hardware for the same amount of money? Absolutely. But that's also missing the point. If you need something pre-built that packs this level of performance into a genuinely portable form factor, the G16 is going to be very hard to beat.
This is one of those laptops where you can actually have your cake and eat it too: desktop levels of performance, a gorgeous OLED display, phenomenal build quality, and enough portability to take it almost anywhere. Asus nailed it. I love this thing!

reviews.title: When the absolute best is required.
reviews.content:
I absolutely love my new laptop. It's powerful, lightweight, and super thin. Yet, runs everything I throw at it flawlessly and handles the heat exceptionally well. It is a gaming machine without looking like a gaming machine. All metal frame, excellent keyboard, and amazing trackpad. It has plenty of ports, so hooking up other devices is quite easy. The display and sound output are the best in the business, hands down, of any laptop. Last thing is the spectacular battey life! Sure, playing any high end games will only net you around 2.5 to 3.5 hours while on battey, but using office apps, browsing the web, or watching YouTube videos will get you a solid 12 to 18 hours of use. Yes, you read that correctly! 

Yeah, this laptop is not cheap, but if you want the best of both worlds, this laptop is the best you can buy.

reviews.title: A Beast of a Machine Packed in a Small Profile
reviews.content: The ASUS - ROG Zephyrus G16 16" OLED 3K Gaming Laptop is nothing short of a lightweight, physically speaking, gaming PC that out boxes its class. What do I mean? When you open this machine for the first time you do not expect it to function as a hardcore gaming computer but Asus has clearly figured it out how to bridge this gap. The moment you start this machine you can already tell that the equipment inside is not second level. It is A tier. The responsiveness with SSD read and write, the multitasking ability it handles with ease, and don't get me started on the gaming experience. You load up your favorite FPS game and away this computer goes. You are not dropping frames, you are not burning your wrists on the keyboard either. The cooling design of the laptop is the only thing that many may have a gripe with. I however do not. You have a machine with so much power and so little space for thermal management that the only way to offset this is a powerful cooling exhaust fan. Yes it will get a bit loud when it runs and you are demanding peak performance from the graphics card and CPU but you also are getting a full on gaming computer in a small form factor. That is not something to complain about but something to marvel at. The battery life also is impressive. I can have this machine playing high demand games and it will not drain extremely fast which is rare for a gaming machine of this profile. As someone who travels a lot this is now my go to machine when I am on the road for work, and in my hotel wanting to play games with friends. This is the standard of portability and gaming all in one.

reviews.title: The Performance Beast at a Cost
reviews.content:
If you are looking for a gaming PC with the best performance you can get, this is it. I’ve had a few high-end gaming PCs, and this is by far the best performing one. It does come at a cost with its high price.

Performance:
As I’ve been saying, this thing performs like a monster. Using email and Internet is almost instantaneous. I know it is simple, but it really is noticeable. There is absolutely no hesitation when using office applications. Running a performance program, this came in at overall score of 99th percentile. The individual results are:
•	CPU: 94th percentile
•	2D graphics: 67th percentile
•	3D graphics: 92nd percentile
•	Memory: 96th percentile
•	Disk: 98th percentile
The fan is normally very quiet and becomes a little louder when gaming, but nothing bothersome or obnoxious. When gaming Forza and Call of Duty, there were absolutely no perceivable frame drops even on the most complicated scenes, using the native resolution of 2560 x 1600.  I was able to get on average mostly 130fps with little dips.

Display and Sound:
This has an OLED screen which is brighter with more vibrant colors and higher contrast. This has very little glare. This is a great looking OLED screen, including the glare, or no glare in this case. This isn’t the best OLED screen I have ever seen, but this is up there. And OLED is really a must have now.
The sound is better than other laptops which usually have very tinny sounds from their very small speakers. These speakers have decent bass and excellent midrange and highs. I don’t know how Asus does it, but they tend to have much better speakers than other manufacturers.


Keyboard and Touchpad:
I find the keyboard easy to type on, and I rarely need to use backspace. It is lighted but is a single RGB zone. For this laptop, I would expect per key RGB lighting. This is not the end of the world, just would be nice to have. There are no movement keys such as Home and End. You must use the Fn+arrow key to do those movements. It has all your standard functions above the function keys and has extra buttons for volume up/down, mic mute, and to bring up the Armoury Crate app.
The touchpad is oversized and is smooth and accurate to use. Although it has your standard touchpad buttons, I always use tapping for the button presses. I have found that tapping is sometimes too sensitive and sometimes not sensitive enough. Can’t really understand it. A little annoying.

Battery and Power:
You get a power brick with a proprietary connecter to power it. It’s 240W and I would call it mid-size. Because of the laptop’s high power, you can’t power or charge it over USB. The battery charges in around an hour. I got around 6 hours when doing office or streaming stuff. This could be a little better. Gaming on battery gives you around 1.5 hours. This is pretty standard and expected. It has a feature that stops charging at 80% to prolong the life of the battery. I’m seeing this more and more on devices and I always turn it on when available.

Wi-Fi and Bluetooth:
The Wi-Fi is the fastest I have seen on any laptop. It has Wi-Fi 7, yet it still performs better. I pay for 2 Gbps internet. With this, I get around 1.9 Gbps download speed and around 900 Mbps upload speed. Before this, the fastest I would ever get on my other devices was around 1.1 Gbps, still fast but not like this. The Bluetooth works as expected. I tried using a pair of B&W headphones and there was no problem pairing them and they kept the connection reliably. I also tried a Scuf controller with the same success.

Connections:
This has your standard connections, HDMI, wired headphones, 2 USB-A, 2 USB-C, and a memory card slot. It also comes with a connection for the power supply which is proprietary.

Memory and SSD:
This laptop includes 32GB of memory, which I find is a good amount to play AAA games. I think 16GB is just not enough. The memory is soldered to the board so there is no way to upgrade it. The SSD that comes with it is 1TB, which is typical for your average mid-range laptop, but for something at this price point, I would have expected 2TB. The other thing to note is that it comes with a secondary SSD slot, but the maximum size drive you can install is 2TB, so no 4TB drive for you. You can upgrade both drives to 2TB to get a total of 4TB that way.

Applications:
This comes with 2 applications, MyAsus and Armoury Crate. To start, I have had no issues running or using either of them. They offer a lot of use and work perfectly, unlike other hardware focused companies I have experienced.
The MyAsus program is used to see system status such as CPU and memory usage, battery level and health, and SSD usage. It has system diagnostics. The following settings are available:
•	Battery care mode (80% charge)
•	360 recording mode
•	Authentic recording
•	Single presenter mode
•	Multi-presenter mode
•	AI noise canceling speaker
•	Task first (prioritize your internet connection’s available bandwidth to particular activities)
•	WiFi smart connect
It also has the ability to do a system update.
The Armoury Crate program shows the same kind of system status of CPU, memory, and GPU usage. You can also see the status of the fans. You can set the operating mode (Windows, Silent, Performance, and Turbo). Aura Sync allows you to sync lighting across Asus devices, and you can also set your light patterns on the PC, but keep in mind that the keyboard is a single RGB zone. Aura Wallpaper allows you to change the wallpaper to some canned available ones. Scenario Profiles allow you to create different profiles that contain settings such as Win key, touch pad, operating mode, Aura sync, slash lighting, lighting brightness. It has macro settings. Game library is where you add your games into a single location. With display settings, you can select default, racing, scenery, RTS/RPG, FPS, cinema, eyecare, vivid, and e-reading.

Conclusion:
This laptop is a performance monster and the ultimate gaming machine that there is very little I can say that is negative about it except I wish it came with a larger SSD because that is now another expense. And I am disappointed that I can’t add a 4TB SSD to it. That would be my biggest complaint. It is rather expensive and more than other gaming laptops with similar specs. I can’t recommend this enough if you want something you can throw any game at, and price is not important.

reviews.title: The Best Zephyrus Yet
reviews.content:
I remember owning the original Zephyrus laptop and a few years later, the first Zephyrus G14. Those laptops were not without some serious quirks, such as the weird keyboard placement on the original and the infamous lack of a webcam on the first G14. The Zephyrus lineup has always been about packing serious gaming performance into a thin and light design, and I feel like the 2026 ASUS ROG Zephyrus G16 is the pinnacle of what ASUS set out to achieve.

As far as the design of the 2026 G16 is concerned, it’s close to perfect. The chassis is CNC-milled aluminum and incredibly thin. It only weighs 4.3 lbs, which is less than my 16” Macbook Pro. It’s remarkable how much ASUS has managed to fit into this package. The keyboard is excellent, largely the same they’ve been using for several generations now, and the oversized glass trackpad is smooth and responsive. For ports, you get two USB-A 3.2 Gen 2 ports, 1 USB-C 3.2 Gen 2 port, and one Thunderbolt 4 USB-C. In addition, there is an HDMI 2.1 connector, a full-size UHS-II SD card reader, and a 3.5mm combo audio jack. Ideally, I would have liked to see Thunderbolt 5, or at least have both USB-C ports support Thunderbolt 4. Note, that there’s no ethernet port, but that’s excusable on something this thin.

The lid sports what ASUS calls “Slash Lighting” which is customizable in their Armoury Crate software. I don’t care too much for this feature, I’m happy to just leave it dark but I did find it neat that you can set it to show the current battery level when you attach the charger. You can also control the single-zone RGB on the keyboard with Armoury Crate.

This model comes with 32GB of speedy LPDDR5X-8533 memory, which is not upgradable, but I’m ok with that on something this thin and light. 32GB is plenty for a gaming machine, especially when the RTX 5080 includes 16GB of its own GDDR7 video memory. A 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD is included, and this is probably my biggest complaint with the hardware configuration. At this price, I’d really like to see a 2TB PCIe 5.0 drive. In practice, PCIe 5.0 is unlikely to make any noticeable difference in gaming, but a 1TB drive fills up extremely quick in modern games. At least the SSD is replaceable, and there is an extra M.2 PCIe slot if you need it.

While ASUS has focused on making the laptop as thin and light as possible, I can’t say the same for the charging brick, as it’s still a brick and weighs over a pound. However, the G16 does support 100w USB-C PD charging, so you can leave the big power brick at home if you are not planning on gaming or using the dedicated GPU. While it is technically possible to game on battery or 100w USB-C power, you’ll need to dramatically lower the graphical settings to achieve comfortable framerates within the reduced power limits. In addition, my testing indicates that it supports passthrough charging over USB-C, allowing the system to run from the USB-C power without affecting the battery longevity.

The screen is easily one of the highlights of the G16. ASUS provides a 16” 2560x1600 OLED panel with a 240hz refresh rate. It’s a thing of beauty. Colors are vibrant, blacks of course are perfect with OLED, and the low 0.2ms response time and fast refresh rate make games look incredibly smooth. It also supports G-Sync, Dolby Vision, and HDR. The 16:10 aspect ratio is what I like to see in modern gaming laptops, as it provides a little bit more vertical real estate. It covers 100% of the DCI-P3 color space, and the brightness levels can reach an astonishing peak of 1100 nits in HDR, achieving VESA DisplayHDR True Black 1000 certification. (although I don’t have any tools to measure the brightness claims)

Just as impressive as the screen is the performance. This model includes the Intel Core Ultra 9 386H and the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080. In this configuration, ASUS uses a large vapor chamber, three fans, and liquid metal thermal compound. The exhaust is vented out the back, keeping warm air away from your hands and cold drinks sitting beside your laptop. Considering how thin the laptop is, I’ve been impressed with the cooling system’s ability to keep all this high-end hardware from getting too toasty. There are several performance profiles in the Armoury Crate software, from Silent to Manual. While the fans are supposed to stay off in Silent mode, I found that they came on from time to time as needed. Turbo mode keeps the fans running and can only be used while plugged in, while Performance can be used for a good balance of noise and power. Manual allows you to crank the system to the absolute max but with minimal gain over Turbo mode. Compared to previous gaming laptops, Turbo is not nearly as loud as you would expect but the sweet spot in my opinion is Performance when it comes to daily gaming.

While the RTX 5080 GPU’s native performance is impressive on its own, adding DLSS upscaling and frame generation can push framerates well into territory that was previously only available on desktops, with incredible visuals and ray tracing in today’s most demanding games. All of the following benchmarks were in Turbo Mode, with the 250w power adapter plugged in and the GPU set to Standard in the Armoury Crate software.

=Geekbench= 
- Single Core: 2659
- Multi-core: 18793

=3Dmark= 
- Time Spy: 18,112 (GPU: 18,704; CPU: 15,386)
- Steel Nomad: 4,535
- Speed Way: 4,779

=Cyberpunk 2077 Phantom Liberty=
- Ultra (DLSS Disabled) 75.79
- Ray Tracing Ultra: 32.59
- Ray Tracing Ultra + DLSS Quality: 51.28
- RT Ultra + DLSS Quality + 4x Multiframe Generation: 160.43

=Doom The Dark Ages (Hebeth level)=
- Ultra Nightmare (Dynamic Resolution off): 68.13
- Ultra Nightmare (DLSS Quality, Path Tracing On): 40.68
- Ultra Nightmare (DLSS Quality, Path Tracing, 4x Frame Gen): 123.89

=Forza Horizon 6=
- Extreme (No Ray tracing) 74 FPS
- Extreme RT – 41 FPS

=Shadow of the Tomb Raider=
- Highest (DLSS Quality) 119 FPS
- Highest (DLSS Quality + RT Ultra): 106 FPS

=Fortnite=
- Direct X Ultra DLSS Ultra 60-70 FPS Avg

I found that Fortnite ran best using its Performance renderer with 50% 3D Resolution and Dynamic 3D enabled. At that setting I was able to maintain a 240 FPS an entire match. An older game, Rocket League, with all settings maxed out had no problems reaching the display’s max refresh rate.

I also played a lot of Halo: Campaign Evolved which was my favorite game as a kid when the original, Combat Evolved, was released on the original Xbox. While I didn’t see a benchmark mode and I didn’t turn on any FPS counters, I played several levels at Ultra settings and never saw anything other than a smooth-running game.

The speakers are by far the best I’ve ever heard on a Windows gaming laptop. For this review, I played solely with the speakers, and not once did I feel like I needed headphones, especially on Performance mode. The speakers remain very clear even at the higher volumes. They are very close in quality to my Macbook Pro speakers which I would consider the gold standard for laptop speakers.

Battery life is surprisingly good for a gaming laptop, making the G16 a great choice as a productivity machine when you aren’t gaming or running heavier workloads such as video editing. With Armoury Crate set to Silent, I streamed 4K YouTube video at 50% brightness and volume and was able to easily get around 10 hours of battery life in two separate tests.  On battery, Armoury Crate defaults display refresh rate to 60Hz and Windows turns off HDR.
 
Pros:
- True Portable Gaming Rig
- Premium Thin and Light Build
- Excellent cooling with tolerable fan noise
- Beautiful 16” 240Hz 2560x1600 OLED 16:10 Display
- VESA DisplayHDR TrueBlack 1000 Certified
- Impressive RTX 5080 performance at up to 160W TGP 
- Outstanding Speakers
- Good port selection and two M.2 Slots
- 100w USB-C charging
- NVIDIA Advanced Optimus and G-SYNC support
- No Bloatware
- Wifi 7 and Bluetooth 6.0
- Windows Hello support
- Fantastic battery life for light use
- ASUS Armoury Crate is useful for performance controls

Cons:
- Expensive
- 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD
- No Thunderbolt 5


Overall – this is the most complete gaming laptop I’ve ever owned. It has everything I want: premium build quality, impressive gaming capability, portability, and an outstanding display. While gaming laptops are crazy expensive in 2026, I feel like this is one that could easily last several years if you are looking for a premium 16” thin and light gaming laptop.

reviews.title: Almost Perfect!
reviews.content:
This compact powerhouse of a laptop is great in many aspects! The 3K OLED screen is so satisfying to game on with its 240Hz refresh rate. The speakers sound great, it's extremely lightweight and portable, and it comes equipped with WiFi 7, so it's future-proof in that aspect. It also comes with 32GB of RAM, though that's non-upgradable. The Intel Ultra 9 285H CPU and RTX 5080 GPU are hugely powerful, making this laptop able to handle anything you throw at it; gaming, video editing, graphic design, and anything else you'd need a laptop for.

I did get the 1TB SSD option, but I already had another drive I wanted to add in the second slot, so it wasn't an issue. Speaking of which, that's one thing I really like — having the option to add a second SSD is vital given how much storage AAA games require.

The only issue I have with this laptop is that the GPU power is capped at 120W. I get that the form factor means it won't get the max power available, but honestly, I'd sacrifice thinness for more power. It's just really disappointing when the rest of the laptop is perfect!

reviews.title: beast of a laptop!
reviews.content:
The Good:
	•	Extremely powerful CPU: The Core Ultra 9 386H is seriously impressive. In my Geekbench testing, it actually outperformed the Core i9-12900K in my desktop, which is remarkable considering how thin and portable this machine is.
	•	Excellent gaming performance: The laptop RTX 5080 obviously isn't going to match a full-power desktop 5080, but it's still an extremely capable GPU. Turbo mode provides an appreciable performance boost when you need everything it has to offer.
	•	Gorgeous OLED display: The 240Hz OLED panel may be my favorite part of the laptop. Blacks are truly black, colors are vibrant, motion is incredibly smooth, and games look fantastic.
	•	Premium build quality: Everything about the G16 feels well manufactured. The aluminum chassis is rigid, clean, and appropriately high-end for a laptop in this price range.
	•	Understated design: ASUS has managed to make a gaming laptop that doesn't scream "gaming laptop." The Eclipse Gray finish and minimalist styling look equally appropriate at home, at work, or in a meeting.
	•	Impressively thin and portable: Considering the hardware inside, the G16 is surprisingly slim and manageable. It feels much closer to carrying a premium productivity laptop than a traditional bulky gaming machine.
	•	Multiple performance modes: Being able to prioritize quiet operation, battery life, or maximum performance is genuinely useful. I can run it conservatively for normal daily use and switch to Turbo when gaming.
	•	Strong battery life for the hardware: You're obviously not buying an RTX 5080 laptop for all-day unplugged gaming, but battery performance during ordinary productivity use is better than I expected.
	•	Excellent keyboard and trackpad: Both feel appropriately premium, with a comfortable keyboard and a large, responsive trackpad that makes the laptop pleasant to use even without a mouse.
	•	Very good speakers: The built-in audio is surprisingly full and clear for such a thin chassis. Headphones are still preferable for gaming, but I rarely feel the need for external speakers during normal use.
	•	Good cooling for its size: ASUS manages to keep some seriously powerful components under control despite the thin chassis. Temperatures are reasonable considering the amount of performance packed inside.
	•	Great all-around machine: Beyond gaming, the combination of a fast CPU, 32GB of memory, excellent display, and powerful GPU makes this equally capable for development, content creation, and general productivity.



The Bad:
	•	Only 1TB of storage: At this price, 2TB really should be standard. Fortunately, the storage can be upgraded, but a premium RTX 5080 laptop shouldn't immediately have me thinking about adding more space.
	•	Turbo mode gets loud: Push the system into Turbo and the fans definitely make themselves known. It's not unusually bad for a high-performance gaming laptop, but headphones are appreciated during demanding games.
	•	It's expensive: There's no getting around the premium price. You're paying not only for the hardware, but also for the thin chassis, OLED screen, materials, and portability.



Overall:
	•	The Zephyrus G16 manages to combine desktop-class levels of performance with the size and build quality of a premium everyday laptop. The fantastic OLED display, powerful Core Ultra 9, RTX 5080, and understated design make it something I can legitimately use as my daily driver rather than just a portable gaming PC. It's expensive and 1TB of storage feels stingy at this level, but the overall package is outstanding and easily earns a 5-star rating.

reviews.content: I bought this about 10 months ago, and for the first six months it was wonderful.  It did everything I needed it to do, I didn't have to worry about viruses, it was easily portable - I was extremely happy.  About months ago I opened it up and the trackpad wasn't working.  Thinking nothing of it, I hard restarted and it was back.  That happened a number of times (probably around 10) until it got to the point I couldn't get it to come back; no matter what I tried, the trackpad was unresponsive.  Thankfully I had an extra mouse that I could use, but having to carry around a peripheral partly defeats the point of a laptop.  When I researched this, I found that this is not an uncommon problem, that the trackpad connection has a tendency to come loose.  "Simply" open up the bottom of the Chromebook, reseat the ribbon connection, and bingo-bango-bongo you'll be up and running.  While the fix is indeed simple enough, once you have the tools to do it, it gets tiring an cumbersome having to do it at least once a week.  And no matter what I've tried to solidly reconnect so it doesn't come loose again, it's continuing to happen.  It's gotten to the point that I don't know if the trackpad will work or not, and if I want to be able to use my laptop, I must carry an external mouse with me.  Very disappointed in the the (lack of) longevity.

q_a.question: Is the 16Gb ram in this laptop is 1 x 16 gb installed or 2 x 8gb installed? Please tell me Asap. And also is there an extra slot or SSD inside the laptop or not?
q_a.answer:
The RAM installed is 2×8GB modules of DDR5-5600. The brand of RAM is Samsung, and the RAM model number is M425R1GB4PB0-CWMOL.

There is only 1×M.2 2280 Gen 4 SSD slot running on x4 channels. The installed brand of SSD installed is Sandisk, which is a 512GB module with the model number SDEPNSJ-5126-1006. Some people have mentioned that their machine has a Samsung M.2 card.

If Upgrading:

Be sure to note that the RAM modules supported are 2×8GB DDR5-5600, 2×16GB DDR5-5600, and 2×32GB DDR5-4800. If you upgrade to the max capacity, you will not be able to use the Overclocked RAM speeds, and the motherboard officially supports DDR5-4800 up to 64GB total or DDR5-5600 [Overclocked] up to 32GB total.

Be sure to note that the maximum supported SSD drive capacity is 4TB, and it must be Gen 4 or earlier, this will support a Gen 5 module, but it will perform at Gen 4 speeds. Do not use a SSD with a heatsink, as it will not fit properly, and will not be cooled properly.

I hope you find this information useful. I do not work for Best Buy and am not associated with them at all. It took trial and error along with research to find the information pertaining to the RAM speeds supported by the motherboard.

q_a.answer: Yes

q_a.answer: From what I gather, there is only 1 M.2 slot for SSDs, but you can clone the existing drive to a larger drive and use that to boot into. If I had to guess, you can put any size M.2 NVME drive (I think it's a 4x4 PCIE M.2 slot), but anything over 2TB is still expensive.

reviews.title: 83ct preferred over amd yoga 7 counterpart
reviews.content:
This particular model bumps to 24gb ram over typical entry point of 16gb, so that's a plus. Like 2 in 1 features too (oled with pen support). 

I also have its amd counterpart (83jr) and there are some things missing there compared to Intel based 83ct that I did not realize before but which are important enough for me to prefer this one.

First, 83jr has a really bad integrated Bluetooth/wifi. Wifi part is fine but Bluetooth is stuttering after waking up from hibernation, which would happen after a few hours of standby . I found no solution to this despite extensive research. Happy to report this Intel box doesn't have this issue.

Second, it has usb4 thunderbolt 4 ports, which works fine with dual 4k docking station that I share with Macbook pro and desktop with tb4 card in it. The 83jr amd chipset only has a dp 2.1 10gbit alt-mode usb 3.2 multi-stream port. In general, dp standards over USB compatibility is a mess, in particular, the multi-stream support. In short you can't have a single docking station that sully supports both thunderbolt and alt mode multi-stream fully. Meaning if you have a tb4 docking for Mac/pcs, this model works fully, but the amd one would require two wires for two displays to work. 
Happily, this 83ct is fully tb4 compatible, so no monitor issues /workarounds.

reviews.title: Macbook Pro 14 M5 Pro w/24GB RAM - 2TB SSD
reviews.content:
What really set this machine aside for me was the 2TB SSD.  I could compromise on the lower end M5 Pro, but SSD space is a requirement for my work flow.

I also noticed a significant increase in WiFi performance from my Macbook Pro 16 M1 Pro.   

The newer machine is faster across the applications I run.  It is ~50% faster when using the Video Encode engine. I actually did an encode without having the unit plugged in to AC mains.  It did consume a percentage of the battery, but, it performed the encode without having to plugin. It also feels faster in browsing and everyday tasks.  Part of this is the increase in WiFi speed.  It's more responsive than the M1, which is the combination of WiFi performance and processor speed.

I like the 14" size because it is just easier to travel with it.  Macbook Pro resolution scaling simply works better than PC's, so the smaller screen did not bother my eyes, it can perform pro level workloads and sips on the battery when browsing and researching information.  I've worked for a full day on the machine and still had over 50% battery left when I got out of the office.  The 14" is also a better lap companion that the 16"; easier to manage.

Another like is the consistent look and feel between the models.  Same chassis, same keyboard, same type of screen.  Just an upgrade of performance and SSD space in the same form factor that I got used to in my M1.

reviews.title: Powerful, Fast, and Worth the Upgrade
reviews.content:
I recently upgraded to the 14-inch MacBook Pro with the M5 Pro chip, 24GB of memory, and 2TB SSD, and so far I’m extremely happy with my purchase.

I use my computer for a little bit of everything—photo and video editing, business, social media content, AI tools, and everyday work—so I needed something that could keep up without slowing down when I have several programs and browser tabs open at once. This MacBook handles multitasking incredibly well. Everything feels fast, smooth, and responsive.

The 14-inch Liquid Retina XDR display is beautiful, especially when working with photos and video. The colors are sharp and vibrant, and the screen size gives me plenty of workspace while still being small enough to carry around easily.

I’m also really glad I chose the 2TB of storage. Photos, videos, editing projects, and business files can take up space quickly, so having the extra storage gives me room to grow without constantly worrying about running out.

And of course, the Space Black finish is gorgeous. It looks sleek, professional, and expensive without being flashy.

This definitely wasn’t a cheap purchase, but I wanted a computer that I wouldn’t outgrow anytime soon. With the M5 Pro chip and 24GB of memory, I feel like I have a machine that can handle what I’m doing now and the businesses and creative projects I’m building for the future.

Overall: 5/5. If you’re a photographer, content creator, entrepreneur, video editor, or someone who does a lot of multitasking, I would absolutely recommend it.

q_a.question: I recently purchased the Lenovo ideal had Slim 3X with the Snapdragon,X-X126100Qualcom processor. When the specs say there are 2 M.2 slots, does this mean they are expansion slots. If not what does 2 M.2 slots mean. Do all SSD laptops have 2 M.2 slots?
q_a.answer:
Hey Rob,

When the specifications list M.2 slots specifically in terms of storage slots, this refers to the types of storage that system will support and how many drives. In this case, the IdeaPad Slim 3x features two M.2 2242 PCIe 4.0 x4 slots, meaning that if one of slots is preoccupied by the included 256GB drive, there is an open storage slot for storage expansion. Also, many modern systems that have SSDs will feature M.2 storage slots, as this form of storage is more compact, efficient, and performant than traditional SSDs.

reviews.title: Powerful, premium, but not perfect
reviews.content:
Product review:
The ROG Zephyrus G16 is one of the best-balanced gaming laptops I’ve used. The OLED display is excellent, the speakers and trackpad are very good, and the overall design feels much more premium and portable than most gaming laptops.

Performance is still very strong and it can handle demanding games at high settings, but there are some compromises. The thin chassis means higher temperatures, noticeable fan noise under load, and the RTX 5080 does not run at the same power level as it does in larger gaming laptops. Battery life is decent for this type of machine, but it still requires some power management if you want to use it away from the charger for several hours.

Overall, I would recommend it to someone who values portability, design, display quality, and strong gaming performance in one device. If your only priority is maximum performance for the money, there are better options, but for a student, traveler, or creator who needs one powerful laptop for everything, the G16 makes a lot of sense.

q_a.question: Does this laptop come with Windows? Do I need it?
q_a.answer: This is a Chromebook that runs the ChromeOS. These devices do not run Windows nor are compatible with Windows. Chromebooks are different from Windows laptop products in that they are designed to be used primarily while connected to the Internet, with most applications and documents living in the cloud. Because of this they don’t have much for on-board storage but they also are not expensive either. Chromebooks run off apps like an Android phone or tablet so you cannot download and install applications or .exe files. If you need to use third party software applications that must be installed on the computer, a Chromebook is likely not for you, where a Windows laptop would suit you better.

reviews.title: Lowk goated laptop
reviews.content:
TLDR: goated laptop
upside: 
INSANE deal for such a display
great specs for a half work half game laptop
chassis feels premium & light (IMO)
downside:
doesn't have a dedicated GPU (people usually get this thing for hype anyways)

As a programmer myself, this might just be overkill for work or studies unless you're training AI or playing literal AAA games, then 16gb ram, intel core ult X7, and 1TB might just be perfect. I personally play games too and it works great. I connect it with my monitor too, and it's running fortnite at 144 fps EASY, can still watch movies and play other mid-tier games with ease (it runs cyberpunk on 60fps, which is just insane for a computer that doesn't have a dedicated GPU). . Everything about the chassis feels great, as it's a full metal build and still feels light. And the best for last: the 16 in OLED touchscreen monitor with a resolution of 2880 x 1800 pixels and 120 hz. This feels absolutely overkill for a "work" laptop, and feels like it can be a standalone machine without the need for an extra monitor and peripherals. 

As I've mentioned before, not having a dedicated GPU is a downside, and the ONLY downside that I can possibly find with this laptop. But to be completely honest, why would you want a dedicated GPU when buying a laptop? 'cause you're way better off building a whole desktop, unless you want to pay an extra $400-600 dollars just for a mid-range GPU, with slightly better air flow to cool GPU (hit or miss), and something 10 times heavier than a normal laptop, not to mention the need to always plug it in because those machines drain out way too quick.

I personally don't think you can find a better deal than this (YET) (I bought this when it had $500 off, so I got it for $1k) for a strong work laptop that can also play games.

reviews.content: This laptop is pretty good, has good battery life, i charge it every night when I play games. Out of the box this laptop was hitting over 90 degrees celsius under no load. I repasted the cpu and it dropped the temps by over 20 degrees (pretty common problem for out of the box laptops. This laptop feels great its lightweight and doesnt weigh my backpack down at all, which is very nice especially when I also have to carry textbooks. Finally power. I went from a gaming laptop with a 3050 to this laptop after it suddenly died, so I was pretty bummed about not being able to play games, however I have found this little guy can be pretty powerful. The Ryzen 7 7730u chips radeon graphics are Vega 8 so it relies heavily on sharing ram with the cpu, so to unlock the best speeds and performance its reccomended to have 32 gb of ram dual channel, thankfully this laptop comes with 1 stick of 16 already so I just popped my other stick of 16 in and now have 32. I can play minecraft, fortnite, btd6, risk of rain 2, black ops 3, among other games. The graphics have to be lowered to lower settings, but I can still play the games with my friends but that means more to me than how the game looks. I only docked a star for the out of the box unfriendlyness for someone who is not good with computers, who might end up being annoyed by the loud fan due to high temps and thermal throttling. However it was not a problem once I repasted it.

reviews.title: Great hardware and value, messy Lenovo software
reviews.content:
I bought the 11-inch Lenovo Idea Tab with 8GB RAM, 128GB storage, Tab Pen and folio case as a birthday gift for a five-year-old who had already outgrown the idea of a basic “kids tablet.” For the price, the hardware package is excellent.

The 2.5K display is sharp and looks very good, performance has been smooth, and 8GB of RAM with 128GB of storage gives it plenty of room to grow. The included pen and folio case add real value instead of feeling like throwaway accessories. It also runs the full Google Play Store and works well with Google Family Link, which was important because I wanted a normal Android tablet that could still be properly supervised.

The biggest negative is Lenovo’s software setup. It came with quite a few unnecessary apps and games installed, and there are a lot of Lenovo-specific menus, gestures, multitasking features and settings that took time to sort through and disable or configure. Some of those features are useful for an experienced user, but they make the initial setup more complicated than it needs to be, especially when configuring the tablet for a child.

Once everything was updated and configured, though, it became a very capable tablet. I would much rather have this than a heavily restricted kids tablet that would be outgrown quickly.

Pros: sharp display, 8GB RAM, 128GB storage, expandable storage, full Android/Google Play support, pen and folio included, good parental-control support.

Cons: too much preinstalled software, unnecessarily complicated Lenovo settings, requires some cleanup during initial setup.

For the price paid, I’m very satisfied with it and think it offers a lot more long-term usefulness than most tablets marketed specifically toward children.

reviews.title: Great Laptop in the Rampocalypse Era
reviews.content:
Long time Lenovo user and thought I should give HP a try for this CPU generation. Very happy with this laptop overall. It has a premium feel and look, and it handles both my work and a heavy gaming load without breaking a sweat. I genuinely couldn’t be happier with the performance and build quality from HP.

The biggest drawback is that HP effectively forces you to use their companion software to access performance profiles. If you do a fresh install of Windows 11 and skip HP’s app, the system will aggressively throttle, so having access to HP’s performance profiles is essential to get the performance you paid for.

I also run Fedora 44 on this machine. As of this writing, onboard sound doesn’t work under Fedora yet, and it will likely require a newer kernel before audio support is fully functional. It also would have been much nicer if this laptop shipped with a 2TB SSD by default, given its performance and price bracket.

Interestingly, I also tried the Omnibook X with the Panther Lake X7, and gaming performance on that weaker configuration was actually better than on this X9 model. Overall, I’m still optimistic this laptop will carry me comfortably through Rampocalypse 2026
